s.b: Everyone who walks through the Gospels, from Mary and Joseph to Pilate and Mary Magdalene.
Towns, regions, lakes, hills and rooms where the story happens, with the events that took place there.
The stories Jesus told, with their themes, where they appear and what they connect to.
Healings, exorcisms, rescues and signs, with where each is told.
What the prophets promised and where the Gospels say it came true.
The events of Jesus’ life in order, each tied to a spot on the map.
Key Greek words from the four Gospels, plus Aramaic phrases and puzzling expressions.
Sin, holiness, love, grace, faith, the kingdom and the other great themes, and how Jesus speaks of each.
The names of God, the titles of Jesus and the Spirit, and the seven “I am” sayings.
The Sabbath, the feasts and the other sacred days that shape the Gospel story.
God’s promises through Noah, Abraham, Moses, David and the new covenant.
Pharisees, Sadducees, the Twelve, tax collectors, the council and the other groups in the story.
Coins, clothing, food, tools and objects mentioned in the Gospels.
Excavated sites, inscriptions and objects that touch the Gospel story.
How people ate, dressed, worshiped, mourned and lived in Jesus’ world.
Rulers, politics, groups and events behind the Gospels.
The voices in the Commentary library, and the terms used in Bible study.
The Bible translations, how they differ, and the manuscripts behind them.

t: A young woman of Nazareth, betrothed to Joseph, who is told by the angel Gabriel that she will bear the Son of the Most High. Luke gives her song, the Magnificat. She is with Jesus at the wedding at Cana and stands near the cross, where he entrusts her to the beloved disciple.
f: Wife of Joseph; relative of Elizabeth

t: A builder (Greek tekton, often rendered “carpenter”) from Nazareth, a descendant of David. In Matthew he obeys dreams to take Mary as his wife, to flee to Egypt and to settle in Nazareth. He disappears from the story after Jesus is twelve.

Son of Zechariah and Elizabeth, he preached repentance in the Judean wilderness and baptized in the Jordan. He pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, rebuked Herod Antipas for his marriage and was beheaded at Machaerus.
f: Son of Zechariah and Elizabeth; relative of Mary

t: An elderly priest of the course of Abijah who is struck silent when Gabriel announces John’s birth in the Temple. His speech returns at the naming of the child, when he sings the Benedictus.
A relative of Mary from a priestly family, who conceives in old age. When Mary visits, the child leaps in her womb and she blesses Mary as “the mother of my Lord”.
f: Wife of Zechariah; relative of Mary

t: The angel who stands in God’s presence, who announces the births of John and Jesus. He also appears in Daniel.
A devout man in Jerusalem who was promised he would see the Messiah. He takes the baby Jesus in his arms and speaks the Nunc Dimittis, warning Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul.
An elderly widow of the tribe of Asher who worshipped night and day in the Temple. She thanks God at the sight of the child and speaks of him to all who await redemption.
The first Roman emperor. Luke dates Jesus’ birth to a census decreed in his reign. Herod the Great ruled Judea as his client king.
Augustus’s successor, in whose fifteenth year (about AD 28–29) John began to preach. His image was on the silver denarius of Jesus’ question about taxes.

A brilliant, brutal builder who rebuilt the Temple, the fortresses of Masada and Herodium, and the port of Caesarea. Matthew shows him trying to kill the child Jesus after the visit of the Magi. He died in 4 BC.

e.u: Tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, 4 BC – AD 39
t: A son of Herod the Great who ruled Galilee through Jesus’ whole ministry. He founded Tiberias, imprisoned and killed John the Baptist, and questioned Jesus before the crucifixion. Jesus called him “that fox”.
f: Husband of Herodias; son of Herod the Great

t: A granddaughter of Herod the Great who left her first husband, Antipas’s half-brother, to marry Antipas. John the Baptist condemned the marriage, and she arranged his death.
The Roman governor who sentenced Jesus to be crucified. Josephus and Philo describe him as harsh and provocative. A building inscription found at Caesarea names him “Prefect of Judea”.
Joseph Caiaphas was high priest through Jesus’ ministry and presided over the trial before the Sanhedrin. A richly decorated ossuary found in Jerusalem in 1990 is inscribed with his family name.
The powerful former high priest (AD 6–15) whose sons and son-in-law held the office after him. John says Jesus was taken to him first.

A fisherman from Bethsaida who lived at Capernaum, brother of Andrew. Jesus renames him “Peter” (the Rock). He confesses Jesus as the Christ, denies him three times, and is restored on the shore of the lake after the resurrection.
A former disciple of John the Baptist who first followed Jesus and brought his brother Peter to him. He brings the boy with loaves and fish and brings Greeks to Jesus.

Fishermen partnered with Peter, nicknamed “Sons of Thunder”. With Peter they are the inner circle at the raising of Jairus’s daughter, the Transfiguration and Gethsemane. Herod Agrippa I executed James around AD 44.
f: Sons of Zebedee and probably Salome

t: Called on the day after Andrew and Peter. He brings Nathanael to Jesus, is asked where to buy bread for the five thousand and asks to see the Father at the Last Supper.
Brought by Philip and astonished that Jesus saw him under the fig tree. He is named at the end of John among the disciples at the lakeshore. Many identify him with the apostle Bartholomew.
A customs agent at Capernaum who left his booth to follow Jesus and hosted a dinner for tax collectors and sinners. Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew; Mark and Luke call him Levi.

Called “the Twin”. He is ready to die with Jesus in John 11, asks “how can we know the way?” and refuses to believe in the resurrection until he sees the marks of the nails, then declares “My Lord and my God!”
The disciples’ treasurer, who agreed to hand Jesus over to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver. Matthew says he returned the silver and hanged himself.
A woman from Magdala whom Jesus had freed of seven demons. She supported his ministry, stood at the cross and was the first to see the risen Lord.
She sat at Jesus’ feet to listen while Martha served. John says she poured expensive perfume on his feet six days before Passover.
Hosted Jesus at Bethany and made the confession “I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God.” John 11 pictures her meeting Jesus on the road after her brother’s death.
Raised from the tomb after four days. The raising prompts the plot to kill Jesus. His tomb is shown at Bethany today. (The poor man in Luke’s parable has the same name but is a different character.)
A woman of means, wife of Chuza, a manager of Herod Antipas’s household, who supported Jesus out of her own funds and was at the empty tomb.
Named by Mark among the women at the cross and the tomb. She is probably the “mother of the sons of Zebedee” in Matthew’s list, who asks Jesus for places for her sons.
f: Probably mother of James and John

e.u: Pharisee and member of the council
t: He comes to Jesus by night, speaks up for him before the council, and after the crucifixion brings about a hundred pounds of spices for the burial.
A rich, righteous member of the council who did not consent to Jesus’ condemnation. He asked Pilate for the body and laid it in his own new tomb.

A short, wealthy toll official who climbed a sycamore-fig to see Jesus. Jesus invited himself to his house, and Zacchaeus promised to give half his goods to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he had cheated.
A leader of a synagogue, probably at Capernaum, who begged Jesus to come and heal his dying twelve-year-old daughter. Jesus raised her up.
Mark names him “son of Timaeus”. He called out to the “Son of David,” was healed and followed Jesus on the road. Matthew mentions two blind men; Luke does not give a name.
A non-Jewish officer, likely in Herod Antipas’s service, who built the local synagogue. He asked Jesus to heal his servant and said “just say the word.” Jesus marveled at his faith.
A Greek woman of Syrian Phoenicia whose daughter was oppressed by a demon. She pressed Jesus to help, saying even the dogs eat the children’s crumbs. Matthew calls her a Canaanite.
A woman who came to draw water at noon at Sychar. Jesus told her about living water and about worship in spirit and truth; she became the first witness to the Samaritans.

e.u: Healed in the country of the Gerasenes
t: A man living among the tombs, with so many spirits that they called themselves “Legion”. After he was healed, Jesus sent him home to tell his own people, and he proclaimed it across the Decapolis.
A widow whose only son was being carried out of the village for burial when Jesus touched the bier and told him to rise.

e.u: Healed at the Pool of Siloam
t: Jesus makes mud, applies it to the man’s eyes and sends him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. His healing leads to a debate with the Pharisees and his own parents.
He lay by the pool with the sick, and Jesus told him to take up his mat and walk. The healing was on a Sabbath.
She put two small copper coins (lepta) into the Temple treasury. Jesus said she had given more than all the rest, because she gave out of her poverty.

e.u: Man who asked about eternal life
t: A wealthy man who had kept the commandments from his youth. Jesus loved him and told him to sell his possessions and follow; he went away grieving.
A man in prison for insurrection and murder. At the Passover amnesty the crowd chose him over Jesus.
A man from the Jewish community of Cyrene, in modern Libya, pressed by the soldiers to carry Jesus’ cross. Mark calls him the father of Alexander and Rufus.

e.u: Disciple on the road to Emmaus
t: One of two followers who walked from Jerusalem on Easter afternoon and failed to recognize Jesus until he broke bread with them.
The officer who watched Jesus die and said, “Truly this man was the Son of God.”
Cited for the Law, the bronze serpent, the manna and the commandment about divorce. He appears with Elijah at the Transfiguration.
The prophet who was expected to return before the Day of the Lord. Jesus says John the Baptist is that Elijah, and Elijah appears with Moses at the Transfiguration.
The patriarch of Genesis. Jesus’ opponents claim him as their father; Jesus says he saw Abraham’s day and, “Before Abraham was, I am.”
Israel’s great king, ancestor of the Messiah. The title “Son of David” appears often; archaeology offers the Tel Dan stele’s mention of the “House of David”.
The prophet Jesus quotes most. Luke has him read from the Isaiah scroll in the Nazareth synagogue, and the Gospels cite him for John the Baptist’s ministry.
Jesus calls his own resurrection after three days “the sign of Jonah” and says the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgement because they repented at Jonah’s preaching.
The builder of the first Temple, celebrated for wisdom and splendor. Jesus says the lilies are more beautiful and that “something greater than Solomon is here”.
The adversary who tempts Jesus in the wilderness, and whom Jesus pictures falling like lightning as God’s kingdom advances. The name means “accuser”.
A fertile, densely settled region ruled by Herod Antipas. Most of Jesus’ ministry took place here, among villages around the lake and on the road between Tiberias and Sepphoris.
The southern region, ruled directly by a Roman prefect from AD 6. It includes Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Bethany, Jericho and the wilderness.
The hill country of the old northern kingdom. Pilgrims often detoured east through the Jordan Valley to avoid it, but Jesus goes through.

A group of ten cities, mostly east of the Jordan, with Greek culture and pagan temples. Scythopolis (Beth Shean) was the only one west of the river. Jesus visits the region and sends a healed man to proclaim the good news there.
The strip of land east of the Jordan, ruled by Antipas. It contained Machaerus, where John was killed, and the place where John had baptized.
Two ancient Phoenician ports in what is now Lebanon, outside Herod’s territory. People from these cities came to hear Jesus, and he withdrew there at one point.

A large Jewish community lived in Egypt, especially in Alexandria. Matthew says Joseph took Mary and the child there to escape Herod and later returned to Nazareth. Coptic tradition places their stay around Old Cairo.
A small farming village in the lower Galilean hills, probably a few hundred people, near the larger city of Sepphoris. Excavations show terraced fields, wine presses and simple houses.

e.u: Town of David, six miles south of Jerusalem
t: A small village in Judea, linked to David and to Micah’s prophecy of a ruler from there. The Church of the Nativity stands over a grotto honored since the 2nd century.

A fishing and farming village on the north shore, with a customs post and a Roman garrison nearby. Jesus taught in its synagogue and healed in Peter’s house. Excavations show black basalt houses and a later white limestone synagogue.
The site of Jesus’ first sign at a wedding and a later healing. Two villages claim the name, Kafr Kanna (traditional) and Khirbet Qana, which has more first-century remains.
A small village on the slope of the Hill of Moreh, where Jesus raised a widow’s son. The village still exists as Nein.

e.u: Fishing village near the lake’s north end
t: The home of Peter, Andrew and Philip. It lay just east of the Jordan in Philip’s territory and was rebuilt as a Greek-style city. The leading candidate is et-Tell.
A basalt town two miles north of Capernaum. Jesus names it with Bethsaida as a city that saw his deeds and did not repent.

e.u: Fishing town on the western shore
t: The home of Mary Magdalene. Excavations have uncovered a first-century synagogue with a carved stone, a market, a harbor and ritual baths. Matthew calls the place Magadan.
A rich crescent of farmland between Magdala and Capernaum, which gave the lake one of its names. Jesus landed here after walking on water, and crowds brought him the sick.

e.u: Pagan city at the foot of Mount Hermon
t: Philip’s capital, built near a spring and a cave shrine of the god Pan. Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ in this region.
A gentile district east of the lake, with a steep bank beside the water. The Gospels name it differently (Gerasa, Gadara, Gergesa), perhaps because the area was linked to more than one city.

e.u: Oasis city in the Jordan Valley
t: One of the oldest cities in the world. Herod built a winter palace on the new site, about two miles from the ancient mound. Jesus heals the blind and visits Zacchaeus here on his way up to Jerusalem.

e.u: Village on the Mount of Olives
t: Home of Lazarus, Martha and Mary, about two miles east of Jerusalem. Jesus stays here during Passion Week.

e.u: Village near the Mount of Olives
t: The village where Jesus sent two disciples to find a colt for his entry into Jerusalem.
Where the risen Jesus broke bread with two disciples. Its location is uncertain, and several sites have been proposed.
A Samaritan village below Mount Gerizim. Jacob’s Well, honored since early times, is the setting for the long talk with the Samaritan woman.
The city whose destruction becomes Jesus’ standard for judgement. Its location is debated, but traditions place it at the southern end of the Dead Sea.
The great Assyrian city on the Tigris, to which Jonah was sent. Jesus holds up its people as examples of repentance.

e.u: Freshwater lake, also Gennesaret and Tiberias
t: About 13 miles long and 8 wide and nearly 700 feet below sea level. It is a harp-shaped lake that supported a fishing industry, with sudden storms funneled down by the hills.
Flows from Mount Hermon through the lake and down to the Dead Sea. John baptized on it, and two sites, Qasr al-Yahud and Al-Maghtas, claim Jesus’ baptism.

e.u: Dry hills between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea
t: A rocky desert of limestone ridges and canyons. John preached here, Jesus fasted here, and the Qumran community withdrew to its edge.
Matthew sets the Sermon on “the mountain” and Luke on “a level place”. Tradition places it on the northern hills above Tabgha, where the Church of the Beatitudes now stands.
The Gospels say only that Jesus took three disciples up “a high mountain”. Tradition since the 4th century says Mount Tabor, while some scholars prefer Mount Hermon.

A city of perhaps 30,000–60,000 people, packed with pilgrims at festivals, built on two ridges around the Temple Mount. It lay about 2,500 feet above sea level, and Gospel writers often say people “go up” to it.

The great sanctuary rebuilt by Herod the Great on a vast platform, with courts for Gentiles, women, Israel and priests. Jesus teaches here, drives out the merchants and predicts its destruction, which came in AD 70.
A ridge across the Kidron Valley from the Temple, where Jesus approached Jerusalem, taught about the end, prayed on the night of his arrest and, in Acts, ascended.
An olive press and garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives. The name means “oil press”. Jesus prayed here and was arrested.
An Aramaic name meaning “skull”, where Jesus was crucified outside the city walls. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre stands on the traditional site.
A double pool with five colonnades near the Sheep Gate, excavated north of the Temple Mount. A man waited here thirty-eight years.

e.u: Pool at the south end of the city
t: A large stepped pool at the end of Hezekiah’s tunnel, where pilgrims purified themselves. The blind man washed here.

A large furnished room in Jerusalem where Jesus ate the Passover meal with his disciples, washed their feet and gave the long farewell talk in John 13–17. The tradition on Mount Zion is old, but the actual house is unknown.
Fortress east of the Dead Sea, built by Herod the Great, where Josephus says John the Baptist was imprisoned and executed. The Gospels say only that Herod Antipas had him imprisoned and beheaded.
A town on the edge of the wilderness north of Jerusalem where Jesus withdrew with his disciples after the raising of Lazarus, before the final Passover.

A village in the hill country west of Jerusalem, by tradition the home of Zechariah and Elizabeth and the birthplace of John the Baptist. Luke says only “a town in Judah.” It is traditionally where Mary visited Elizabeth and sang the Magnificat.
A place with plenty of water where John the Baptist was baptizing, near Salim. Its exact location is debated.

On the east shore of the Sea of Galilee, a site with a Byzantine monastery and church built on a steep slope by the shore. Tradition connects it with the healing of the man from the tombs and the herd of pigs rushing into the lake.

A Roman fortress at the northwest corner of the temple courts, built by Herod the Great, where soldiers watched over the crowds. Tradition has placed Pilate’s judgment hall near it, though some scholars place the trial at Herod’s palace.
A covered walkway along the east side of the temple courts. Jesus walked here at the Feast of Dedication, and the apostles later gathered here.
The “potter’s field” bought with the thirty pieces of silver Judas threw into the temple. Matthew says it was called the Field of Blood. It is in the Hinnom Valley south of the Old City.
The home of the high priest in Jerusalem, where Jesus was taken for questioning and where Peter denied him three times.
A rounded mountain in Lower Galilee, traditionally the Mount of Transfiguration. The Gospels do not name the mountain, and some think Mount Hermon is more likely.
A settlement on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea near the caves where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found, linked by many scholars with the Essenes.

A farmer scatters seed on a path, rocky ground, thorns and good soil. Only the good soil bears a crop. Jesus explains that the seed is the word of the kingdom and the soils are the different ways people hear it.

An enemy sows weeds in a field of wheat. The master tells his servants to let both grow until the harvest, when they will be separated. Jesus explains it as the end of the age, when the angels sort the righteous from the wicked.
The smallest of seeds grows into the largest garden plant, big enough for birds to nest in its branches. The kingdom begins small and becomes large.
A woman mixes a little yeast into a large amount of flour until all of it is worked through. The kingdom spreads quietly from within.
A man scatters seed and goes about his life while it sprouts and grows without his understanding how. When the grain is ripe he puts in the sickle. Only Mark tells this one.
A man finds treasure in a field, hides it again, and in his joy sells everything to buy the field. The kingdom is worth everything.
A merchant looking for fine pearls finds one of great value and sells everything he has to buy it.
A net is thrown into the sea and gathers fish of every kind. The good are kept and the bad are thrown away, as the angels will separate the righteous from the wicked at the end of the age.
One man builds his house on rock and another on sand. When the storm comes, only the house on the rock stands. Hearing Jesus’ words and doing them is the rock.
A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find the one that is lost, and rejoices when he finds it. There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.
A woman with ten silver coins loses one, lights a lamp, sweeps the house and searches until she finds it, then calls her friends to celebrate. Only Luke tells this one.

A younger son takes his inheritance, wastes it far from home, and returns hoping to be a hired servant. His father runs to meet him, restores him as a son and throws a feast, while the older brother resents it. Often called the parable of the loving father or the two sons.
A king forgives a servant a huge debt. That servant then refuses to forgive a fellow servant a small one and is handed over for punishment. Jesus tells it after Peter asks how many times to forgive.
A moneylender cancels the debts of two men, one owing ten times what the other owed. Jesus asks Simon the Pharisee which will love him more, and applies it to the woman who anointed his feet.
A man beaten by robbers is passed by a priest and a Levite. A Samaritan stops, cares for him and pays for his recovery. Jesus tells it in answer to the lawyer’s question, “Who is my neighbor?”

A landowner hires workers at different hours and pays all of them a denarius. Those who worked all day complain, and he answers that he is free to be generous. The last will be first and the first last.
A father asks two sons to work in the vineyard. One says no and goes anyway; the other says yes and does not go. Tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom ahead of the chief priests.

A landowner sends servants and finally his son to collect fruit from his vineyard, and the tenants kill them. Jesus quotes Psalm 118: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The religious leaders realize he is speaking about them.
A king invites guests to his son’s wedding. They refuse and some mistreat his servants, so he opens the invitation to everyone in the streets. One guest without wedding clothes is thrown out.

A man prepares a great banquet but invited guests all make excuses. He brings in the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame, and then people from the roads. Luke’s version is told at the table of a leading Pharisee.
Seeing guests choose the best seats, Jesus says to take the lowest place and let the host move you up. Those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.

e.n: The cost of building a tower
t: Before building a tower or going to war, a person sits down to count the cost. Anyone who would follow Jesus should do the same.
Ten bridesmaids wait for the bridegroom. Five bring extra oil and five do not, and when he arrives at midnight the unprepared are shut out. The lesson: stay awake and be ready.
A master gives his servants five, two and one talent before traveling. Two put the money to work; the third buries his. On return, the faithful are rewarded and the fearful servant loses what he had.
A nobleman leaves to receive a kingdom and gives ten servants a mina each. Luke tells it near Jericho, as people think the kingdom is about to appear, and it includes citizens who refuse the king.

The Son of Man separates the nations like a shepherd dividing sheep from goats. What was done, or not done, for the hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick and imprisoned was done, or not done, to him.

A servant left in charge of the household is blessed if the master finds him faithful on his return, and punished if he has abused the others. Jesus calls the disciples to stay ready for a day they do not know.
A man leaves home and tells his doorkeeper to stay alert, because no one knows when the master of the house will return. “Watch.”
When a fig tree puts out leaves, you know that summer is near. In the same way, when you see the signs Jesus described, know that the end is near.
A man comes looking for fruit on his fig tree for three years and finds none. The gardener asks for one more year to dig around it and fertilize it. If it still bears no fruit, then cut it down.
A man knocks on his neighbor’s door at midnight to borrow bread for a guest. The neighbor gets up because of the man’s persistence. How much more will the Father give to those who ask?
A widow keeps demanding justice from a judge who neither fears God nor respects people, and he finally gives it to her. Jesus tells it so that his followers will pray and not lose heart.

e.n: The Pharisee and the tax collector
t: Two men pray in the temple. The Pharisee thanks God that he is not like other people; the tax collector beats his chest and asks for mercy. The tax collector goes home justified.

A wealthy farmer plans to build bigger barns and take life easy. God says, “This night your soul is required of you.” Life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. Jesus tells it in answer to a man who wanted him to settle an inheritance dispute.

A manager about to lose his job quickly reduces what his master’s debtors owe so that they will welcome him later. His master praises his shrewdness. Jesus ends with the saying about two masters: you cannot serve God and money.

A rich man ignores the beggar Lazarus at his gate. After death, Lazarus is comforted and the rich man is in torment, and Abraham says that if they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they would not be persuaded even if someone rose from the dead.
A servant who comes in from the field does not expect to be thanked for doing his duty. When you have done all that you were told, say, “We are unworthy servants.”
No one lights a lamp and hides it under a basket. It is put on a stand so that everyone can see. What is hidden will be brought to light.
No one sews a patch of new cloth on an old garment or pours new wine into old wineskins, or both will be ruined. Jesus says this when asked why his disciples do not fast.

Children call out to one another, “We played the flute and you did not dance.” Jesus says this generation rejected both John the Baptist, who came fasting, and the Son of Man, who came eating and drinking.
No one can plunder a strong man’s house unless he first ties him up. Jesus tells this when accused of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebul.

e.n: The return of the unclean spirit
t: When an unclean spirit leaves a person, it wanders, then returns with seven worse spirits to find the house swept and empty. A cleaned life with nothing in it is not safe.
John records a figure of speech rather than a parable: the shepherd enters by the door, calls his sheep by name, and lays down his life for them. Jesus says, “I am the good shepherd.”
Jesus says, “I am the true vine.” Branches that remain in him bear fruit, and branches that do not are cut off. John also calls this a figure of speech.
When the disciples ask why he speaks in parables, Jesus says the secrets of the kingdom are given to them, while those outside see and do not see. He quotes Isaiah 6:9-10.

At a wedding in Cana, the wine runs out. Jesus has servants fill six stone jars with water, and it becomes wine better than what was served first. John calls it the first of his signs, and it revealed his glory.
A royal official from Capernaum asks Jesus to come heal his dying son. Jesus tells him, “Go, your son will live,” and the boy recovers at the same hour. John calls it the second sign in Galilee.
After a night of catching nothing, Simon Peter lets down his nets at Jesus’ word and nearly breaks them with fish. He falls at Jesus’ knees and Jesus calls him to catch people.

e.n: The man with an unclean spirit
t: In the synagogue at Capernaum, a man cries out, “I know who you are, the Holy One of God.” Jesus commands the spirit to be silent and come out, and the crowd marvels at his authority.
Simon’s mother-in-law lies sick with a fever. Jesus takes her hand and lifts her up, the fever leaves, and she begins to serve them.
A man with leprosy kneels and says, “If you are willing, you can make me clean.” Jesus touches him and says, “I am willing; be clean,” and tells him to show himself to the priest.

e.n: The paralyzed man lowered through the roof
t: Four friends dig through a roof to lower a paralyzed man to Jesus. Jesus says, “Your sins are forgiven,” then heals him to show that the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins.

e.n: The man at the pool of Bethesda
t: A man who has been ill thirty-eight years lies by the pool in Jerusalem. Jesus tells him to take up his mat and walk. It was a Sabbath, which started the controversy that John records afterward.

e.n: The man with the withered hand
t: On a Sabbath in the synagogue, Jesus asks whether it is lawful to do good or to do harm on the Sabbath. He heals the man’s hand, and his opponents begin to plan against him.

A Roman centurion asks Jesus to heal his servant but says he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof; Jesus only needs to speak the word. Jesus marvels, “Not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

e.n: The widow’s son raised at Nain
t: At the gate of Nain, Jesus meets a funeral procession for a widow’s only son. He touches the bier, says, “Young man, arise,” and gives him back to his mother.
A storm swamps the disciples’ boat while Jesus sleeps in the stern. He rebukes the wind and sea, and there is a great calm. The disciples ask, “Who then is this?”
A man possessed by a legion of spirits lives among the tombs in the region of the Gerasenes. Jesus sends the spirits into a herd of pigs, and the man is found sitting, clothed and in his right mind.
A synagogue ruler begs Jesus to heal his dying daughter. News comes that she has died, but Jesus says, “Do not fear, only believe,” takes her hand and says, “Talitha cumi.” The girl gets up.

e.n: The woman who touched Jesus’ cloak
t: A woman who has bled for twelve years pushes through the crowd and touches Jesus’ cloak. Power goes out from him. He says, “Daughter, your faith has made you well.”
Two blind men follow Jesus calling, “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” He touches their eyes and says, “According to your faith let it be done to you.”
After Jesus casts out a demon from a man who could not speak, the man speaks. The crowds marvel, while the Pharisees say he casts out demons by the prince of demons.

With five loaves and two fish, Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand men on a grassy hillside and the disciples gather twelve baskets of leftovers. It is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, recorded in all four Gospels.
In the fourth watch of the night, Jesus comes to the disciples walking on the lake. In Matthew, Peter steps out on the water and begins to sink. When Jesus enters the boat, the wind stops.
People bring the sick on mats to Gennesaret, and as many as touch the fringe of his cloak are healed.
A Gentile woman near Tyre persists in asking Jesus to heal her daughter, even answering that “even the dogs eat the crumbs.” Jesus honors her faith and the girl is healed from a distance.
In the Decapolis, Jesus puts his fingers in the ears of a deaf man with a speech impediment, touches his tongue and says, “Ephphatha” (be opened). Mark preserves the Aramaic word.
With seven loaves and a few small fish, Jesus feeds four thousand men, and they collect seven baskets of leftovers. It happens in a largely Gentile region.

Jesus leads a blind man out of the village, spits on his eyes and lays hands on him. The man first sees people “like trees walking,” then Jesus touches him again and he sees clearly. Only Mark records it.

On a high mountain, Jesus’ face shines like the sun and his clothes become white. Moses and Elijah appear and speak with him, and a voice from the cloud says, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” Not usually counted as a healing, but it is one of the Gospels’ great revelations of his glory.

e.n: The boy with an unclean spirit
t: At the foot of the mountain, a father brings his son, whom the disciples could not heal. “I believe; help my unbelief!” Jesus rebukes the spirit and the boy is healed. This kind comes out only through prayer.

e.n: The coin in the fish’s mouth
t: When collectors ask whether Jesus pays the temple tax, he sends Peter to the lake to catch a fish with a coin in its mouth, enough for both of them. Only Matthew tells this one.

Jesus makes mud with spit, puts it on a man’s eyes and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam. The man sees. The Pharisees interrogate him and put him out of the synagogue, and Jesus tells them, “I am the light of the world.”

On a Sabbath in a synagogue, Jesus lays hands on a woman who has been bent over for eighteen years, and she stands up straight and praises God. He answers the synagogue ruler’s protest by pointing to how people water their animals on the Sabbath.
At a meal at a leading Pharisee’s house on the Sabbath, Jesus heals a man with swollen limbs and asks whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath.
Ten men with leprosy cry out for mercy and are healed on their way to the priests. Only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank Jesus.

Lazarus of Bethany has been dead four days when Jesus arrives. He says, “I am the resurrection and the life,” weeps at the tomb, and cries, “Lazarus, come out.” John says this event led the leaders to plot Jesus’ death.
A blind beggar by the road near Jericho shouts, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” and will not be silenced. Jesus calls him, asks what he wants, and restores his sight.

e.n: The cursing of the fig tree
t: Jesus finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit and says it will never bear fruit again. The next morning it has withered. Mark frames it around the cleansing of the temple.
When a disciple strikes the high priest’s servant with a sword in Gethsemane, Jesus says, “No more of this,” and touches the man’s ear and heals him. John names the servant Malchus.

e.n: The second great catch of fish
t: After the resurrection, seven disciples fish all night without success. A man on the shore tells them to cast on the right side and they catch 153 large fish. John says they recognize the Lord, and Jesus has already made breakfast on a charcoal fire.

On the third day, the tomb is empty and Jesus appears to the women, to the disciples and to many others. All four Gospels end with it, and the rest of the New Testament proclaims it. Not a miracle he performed on someone else, but the sign to which all the others point.
Isaiah told King Ahaz that a young woman would conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, “God with us.” Matthew applies it to Mary and the birth of Jesus.
Micah named Bethlehem Ephrathah as the place from which a ruler of Israel would come. The chief priests and scribes quote it to Herod when the Magi ask where the king is to be born.
God promised David that his throne and kingdom would be established forever through his offspring. The Gospels open by tracing Jesus to David.
God told Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring. Matthew begins with “the son of Abraham,” and Mary and Zechariah both sing of this promise.
Hosea wrote of Israel, “Out of Egypt I called my son.” Matthew sees Jesus’ return from Egypt as a replay of Israel’s story and applies the verse to him.
Jeremiah pictured Rachel weeping for her children as they went into exile. Matthew hears it again in the grief of Bethlehem’s mothers after Herod’s massacre.

e.n: He will be called a Nazarene
t: Matthew says the prophets said Jesus would be called a Nazarene, but no single Old Testament verse says this. Many link it to the Hebrew word for “branch” (netzer) in Isaiah 11:1, or to the low esteem of Nazareth.
Isaiah spoke of a voice crying out in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord. All four Gospels identify this voice with John the Baptist.

e.n: The messenger who prepares the way
t: Malachi promised a messenger to prepare the way before the Lord. Jesus says John is this messenger.

Malachi said God would send Elijah before the great and terrible day of the Lord. Jesus says that Elijah has come in John the Baptist, and the angel Gabriel tells Zechariah that John will go in the spirit and power of Elijah.
Isaiah said that the people in darkness in Zebulun and Naphtali, the land by the sea, would see a great light. Matthew applies it to Jesus starting his ministry in Capernaum.

e.n: The Spirit upon the anointed one
t: Isaiah wrote of one anointed to preach good news to the poor and proclaim freedom for captives. In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus reads this passage and says, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
After Jesus heals many in Capernaum, Matthew says this fulfilled Isaiah’s words that the servant took up our infirmities and bore our diseases.

Isaiah’s servant would not quarrel or cry out, would not break a bruised reed, and would bring justice to the nations. Matthew quotes it when Jesus heals the crowds and asks them not to make him known.
God told Isaiah that the people would hear and not understand, see and not perceive. Jesus quotes it to explain why he teaches in parables, and John uses it to explain why many did not believe.

Moses told Israel that God would raise up a prophet like him from among them, and that they should listen to him. In the Gospels people ask whether Jesus is “the Prophet,” and the voice at the transfiguration says, “Listen to him.”

In the wilderness, Moses lifted a bronze serpent on a pole and everyone who looked at it was healed. Jesus tells Nicodemus that the Son of Man must be lifted up in the same way, so that everyone who believes may have eternal life.

God gave Israel manna in the wilderness. After the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus says the true bread from heaven is not what Moses gave but what his Father gives, and then, “I am the bread of life.”

The prophets pictured water poured out on the thirsty land and rivers flowing from the temple. At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus cries, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” and John explains it as the Spirit.
Ezekiel condemned Israel’s false shepherds and promised that God would shepherd his sheep himself and set one shepherd over them. Jesus calls himself the good shepherd.
Jeremiah promised a new covenant in which God would write his law on people’s hearts and forgive their sins. At the Last Supper, Jesus gives the cup as the new covenant in his blood.
Zechariah told Jerusalem that her king would come humble and riding on a donkey. Matthew and John both describe Jesus entering the city this way.
The crowds greet Jesus with words from Psalm 118: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Jesus later tells Jerusalem they will not see him again until they say it.
Psalm 118 speaks of a stone the builders rejected that became the cornerstone. Jesus quotes it after the parable of the tenants, and the leaders realize he is speaking of them.

Isaiah called the temple a house of prayer for all nations, and Jeremiah called it a den of robbers when it was misused. Jesus combines the two when he drives out those buying and selling in the temple.
The psalmist laments that even his close friend, who ate his bread, has lifted his heel against him. At the Last Supper, Jesus applies it to the one who would betray him.
Zechariah was paid thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the Lord. Matthew connects this with Judas’ payment and the purchase of the potter’s field.
Zechariah wrote, “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.” On the way to Gethsemane, Jesus tells the disciples that all will fall away.
Isaiah’s servant was led like a lamb to the slaughter and did not open his mouth. Before Pilate and the high priest, Jesus mostly stays silent.
The servant in Isaiah gives his back to those who strike him and does not hide his face from mocking and spitting. The Gospels describe the guards and the soldiers doing exactly this to Jesus.
Isaiah says the servant was counted among transgressors. Jesus quotes it at the Last Supper, and he is crucified between two criminals.
The psalmists complain of enemies who hate them without a cause. Jesus tells the disciples that it is written in their law that people hated him without a cause.

e.n: My God, why have you forsaken me?
t: On the cross, Jesus cries out the first line of Psalm 22 in Aramaic: “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani.” That psalm also describes mocking crowds, pierced hands and feet, and the dividing of garments.
Psalm 22 describes the sufferer’s garments being divided and lots cast for his clothing. John says the soldiers who crucified Jesus did exactly this.
The sufferer in Psalm 22 is mocked: “He trusts in the Lord; let him deliver him.” The chief priests, scribes and elders say nearly the same words to Jesus on the cross.
The psalmist says that for his thirst they gave him vinegar to drink. On the cross, Jesus says, “I thirst,” and a sponge of sour wine is lifted to him on a hyssop branch.
The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken, and the psalmist says the righteous person’s bones are kept. John notes that the soldiers did not break Jesus’ legs.

e.n: They will look on the one they pierced
t: Zechariah says the people would look on the one they pierced and mourn. John sees it in the soldier’s spear thrust into Jesus’ side.
Isaiah says the servant was assigned a grave with the wicked but was with a rich man in his death. Jesus is buried in the new tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man.

Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12 describes a servant who is despised, bears the sins of many and is exalted. The Gospel writers apply parts of this passage to Jesus again and again, and Jesus himself says it must be fulfilled in him.

Jonah spent three days in the belly of the great fish. Jesus tells those asking for a sign that the only sign they will be given is the sign of Jonah, and that as Jonah was in the fish three days and nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth.

David wrote that God would not abandon his holy one to the grave. On Easter evening, Jesus tells the disciples that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms had to be fulfilled, and that the Messiah would suffer and rise on the third day.

e.n: The Son of Man coming with the clouds
t: Daniel saw one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven and receiving an everlasting kingdom. Jesus applies this to himself before the high priest and in his teaching on the end.
Daniel spoke of an abomination that causes desolation set up in the holy place. Jesus tells the disciples that when they see this in the temple, those in Judea should flee to the mountains.

Psalm 110 begins, “The Lord says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” Jesus asks how the Christ can be both David’s son and David’s Lord, and later tells the high priest that the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of Power.

Jesus says he has not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them, and after the resurrection he says all that was written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.
Isaiah says all your children will be taught by the Lord. Jesus quotes it in the bread of life discourse: everyone who hears and learns from the Father comes to him.

e.n: An angel promises John the Baptist’s birth
t: The priest Zechariah is serving in the temple when Gabriel tells him that his aged wife Elizabeth will bear the forerunner of the Lord.

e.n: The angel Gabriel appears to Mary
t: Mary, engaged to Joseph, is told she will conceive and bear the Son of the Most High, and she answers, “Let it be to me according to your word.”
Mary travels south to Elizabeth, whose baby leaps at her greeting, and Mary answers with the song traditionally called the Magnificat.
The hill-country town is not named; Ein Karem is the traditional site.
f: Ein Karem, hill country of Judea

t: Elizabeth’s son is born and named John, and Zechariah, able to speak again, prophesies about his son and the coming salvation.
Town not named; Ein Karem is the traditional site.
Because of a Roman census Joseph and Mary go to David’s town, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger.
Angels announce to shepherds in the fields that a Savior has been born, and the shepherds go and find the baby.
Traditional site near Beit Sahour; the fields are not named.
Eastern wise men follow a star, ask Herod in Jerusalem where the king of the Jews is to be born, and worship the child with gifts.
Mary and Joseph bring the baby to the temple, where Simeon and Anna recognize him as the promised salvation.
Warned in a dream, Joseph takes Mary and Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod.
Exact place in Egypt is not given; this pin marks the country generally.

e.n: Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem
t: Herod, tricked by the Magi, orders the boys of Bethlehem killed, which Matthew links to Jeremiah’s mourning at Ramah.
After Herod’s death the family returns from Egypt and makes its home in Galilee, in Nazareth.

e.n: The boy Jesus in the Temple
t: At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple, and his parents find him listening to the teachers and asking questions.

e.n: John the Baptist preaches in the wilderness
t: John calls Israel to repent and be baptized, and says that someone far greater is coming after him.
Traditionally Bethany beyond the Jordan (Al-Maghtas); the exact spot is debated.
Jesus is baptized by John, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father’s voice calls him his beloved Son.
Traditional site; the exact location is debated.

e.n: Jesus is tempted in the wilderness
t: After forty days of fasting, Jesus resists the devil’s three temptations by quoting Scripture.
Traditional Mount of Temptation near Jericho; the wilderness spot is not named.
Andrew, another disciple, Peter, Philip and Nathanael begin following Jesus after John points him out as the Lamb of God.
Site debated.
At a village wedding Jesus turns water into wine, the first of the signs John records.
Kafr Kanna is the traditional site; Khirbet Qana is another candidate.
Jesus drives out the money changers and sellers and speaks of raising up the temple of his body in three days.
A Pharisee and member of the council comes by night, and Jesus tells him he must be born again and that God so loved the world.
Exact house not named.
Jesus’ disciples baptize in Judea while John baptizes at Aenon, and John says of Jesus, “He must increase, but I must decrease.”
Site debated.
Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for water and offers her living water, and many in the town come to believe.
A royal official begs Jesus to heal his dying son at Capernaum, and Jesus says, “Go; your son will live,” from Cana.
Hearing that John has been arrested, Jesus goes to Galilee and makes Capernaum his base, preaching that the kingdom is near.
In his hometown synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah and says it is fulfilled today, but the people turn against him.
Jesus calls Simon, Andrew, James and John to leave their nets and follow him, and Luke places this after a huge catch of fish.
Luke names the lake of Gennesaret; the exact shore is not named.
Jesus teaches with authority and drives an unclean spirit out of a man in the synagogue.

e.n: Peter’s mother-in-law and the evening healings
t: Jesus heals Peter’s mother-in-law, and that evening the whole town gathers at the door for healing.
Jesus travels through the towns of Galilee teaching, preaching and healing, and large crowds follow him.
Region marker; no single town.
A man with leprosy kneels and asks to be made clean, and Jesus touches him and heals him.
Town not named.

e.n: The paralytic lowered through the roof
t: Four friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof, and Jesus forgives his sins and heals him.

e.n: Jesus calls Matthew and eats with sinners
t: Jesus calls the tax collector Levi (Matthew) and dines with tax collectors and sinners, saying he came for the sick.

e.n: Healing at the pool of Bethesda
t: On a Sabbath Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, then explains his relationship to the Father.

e.n: Lord of the Sabbath in the grainfields
t: When the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, Jesus calls himself Lord of the Sabbath.
Field not named.

e.n: The man with the withered hand
t: Jesus heals a man’s withered hand on the Sabbath in a synagogue, and his opponents begin to plot against him.
Town not named.
After a night in prayer, Jesus names twelve disciples as apostles.
The mountain is not named.
Jesus teaches the Beatitudes, the Lord’s Prayer and much more; Luke’s parallel is set on a level place.
Traditional site.
A Roman centurion asks Jesus to heal his servant without coming to his house, and Jesus marvels at his faith.
At the gate of Nain Jesus stops a funeral and tells a widow’s dead son to rise.
After a healing, Jesus’ critics say he casts out demons by the prince of demons, and he answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand.
Setting is “the house” in Mark.
When his mother and brothers come for him, Jesus says that those who do God’s will are his family.
From a boat Jesus teaches the crowds in parables, including the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed and the yeast.
Traditional spot at Tabgha.
f: Shore of the Sea of Galilee

t: A violent squall hits the boat, and Jesus calms the wind and waves with a word.
Jesus frees a man from a legion of demons, who enter a herd of pigs that rushes into the lake.
Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes appear in the manuscripts; Kursi is the usual site.
f: Kursi, east shore of the lake

e.n: Jairus’ daughter and the woman with bleeding
t: On the way to Jairus’ house a woman is healed by touching Jesus’ cloak, and Jesus then raises Jairus’ daughter.
Town implied by the context.

e.n: Woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum
t: Jesus warns the towns where most of his miracles were done that they will face judgment if they do not repent.
Jesus sends the Twelve in pairs to preach and heal, with instructions about what to carry and how to respond to rejection.
Region marker.

e.n: John the Baptist is imprisoned and killed
t: Herod Antipas imprisons John for rebuking his marriage, and John is beheaded at Herodias’ request.
Josephus names Machaerus as the prison; the Gospels do not.
With five loaves and two fish Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand men, the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels.
Luke names Bethsaida; the exact site is debated.
Jesus comes to the disciples across the stormy lake, and Peter briefly walks toward him.
People bring the sick to touch the edge of Jesus’ cloak, and all who touch him are healed.
The crowd finds Jesus at Capernaum, and he says he is the bread of life; many disciples turn back at this teaching.
Pharisees ask why the disciples ignore tradition, and Jesus says what defiles a person comes from the heart.
Place not named.
Jesus enters Gentile territory, and a woman’s persistent faith leads him to heal her daughter.

e.n: Healing the deaf man in the Decapolis
t: Jesus heals a deaf man who could hardly speak, and many other sick people, in Gentile country.
Region marker.
A second large crowd is fed with seven loaves and a few fish.
Exact site not named.
Jesus lands at Magadan (Magdala or Dalmanutha) and refuses the Pharisees’ request for a sign.
Mark’s Dalmanutha is uncertain.

e.n: A blind man healed at Bethsaida
t: Jesus heals a blind man in two stages, in a story only Mark records.
Peter says Jesus is the Christ, and Jesus begins to speak of his coming suffering.
On a high mountain Jesus shines with glory and speaks with Moses and Elijah, and the Father calls him his Son.
Tradition favors Tabor; some scholars prefer Mount Hermon.

e.n: Jesus heals a boy with a spirit
t: Jesus casts out a spirit that the disciples could not, saying some kinds need prayer.
Place not named.

e.n: The temple tax and the coin in the fish
t: Asked about the temple tax, Jesus sends Peter to catch a fish with a coin in its mouth.
The disciples argue about who is greatest, and Jesus teaches humility, care for little ones and forgiveness.

e.n: Jesus teaches at the Feast of Tabernacles
t: At the autumn feast Jesus teaches in the temple, invites the thirsty to come to him, and sends away the accusers of a woman caught in adultery.

e.n: “I am the light of the world”
t: Jesus says he is the light of the world and that before Abraham was, he is.
Jesus sends a blind man to wash at Siloam and he sees, which leads to a sharp dispute with the Pharisees.
Jesus says he is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.
Setting continues from the Jerusalem feast.
Setting his face toward Jerusalem, Jesus is turned away by a Samaritan village, and he rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire.
Village not named.
Jesus sends seventy-two ahead of him in pairs, and they return with joy.
Region marker.
Asked who his neighbor is, Jesus tells of a Samaritan who helps a man beaten on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho.
Told as a parable on the road down to Jericho.
Martha is busy serving while Mary sits at Jesus’ feet, and Jesus says Mary has chosen the better part.
Luke says only “a village”; Bethany is the traditional identification.
At the winter feast Jesus says he and the Father are one, and the crowd tries to stone him.
Jesus weeps and then calls Lazarus out of the tomb after four days.
After Lazarus is raised, the chief priests and Caiaphas decide Jesus must die.
Because of the plot, Jesus leaves public view and stays with his disciples in a town called Ephraim.
Site identified with et-Taybeh.
Ten men with leprosy are healed, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank Jesus.
Pharisees test Jesus about divorce, and he points back to God’s design in creation.
Region marker.
Jesus welcomes children and says the kingdom belongs to such as these.
Region marker.
A rich man asks how to inherit eternal life and goes away sad when Jesus tells him to sell all.
Region marker.
Jesus tells the Twelve for the third time that he will be killed and rise, and he teaches that greatness is serving.
Region marker.
As Jesus leaves Jericho a blind beggar cries out to him and receives his sight.
Matthew mentions two men.
Jesus invites himself to the house of the chief tax collector Zacchaeus, who gives half his goods to the poor.
A woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus shortly before his death, and he says she has prepared him for burial.
Matthew and Mark place it in the house of Simon the leper.
Riding a donkey, Jesus enters Jerusalem to cries of “Hosanna” from the crowds.
f: Bethphage and the Mount of Olives

t: Jesus curses a fruitless fig tree, and the next day it has withered; he uses this to teach about faith.
Jesus overturns the money changers’ tables, saying the temple should be a house of prayer.

e.n: Questions and teaching in the Temple
t: Leaders challenge Jesus’ authority, and he answers about taxes, the resurrection and the greatest commandment.

e.n: Some Greeks ask to see Jesus
t: Greeks come to Philip wanting to see Jesus, and he speaks of the grain of wheat that must die and of being lifted up.

e.n: Woes on the scribes and Pharisees
t: Jesus sharply warns against the religious leaders’ hypocrisy and laments over Jerusalem.
Jesus watches the crowd give and says a poor widow gave more than all the rest.
On the Mount of Olives Jesus speaks of the temple’s fall, coming trials and his return, and tells parables about being ready.
Judas goes to the chief priests and agrees to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver.
At the Passover meal Jesus washes his disciples’ feet, gives them the bread and cup, and says one of them will betray him.
Traditional site of the Upper Room.
Jesus comforts his disciples, promises the Spirit and says he is the vine and they are the branches.
Traditional site; the last parts are spoken on the way.
Jesus prays for himself, his disciples and all who will believe through them.
Exact place not named; spoken before crossing the Kidron.
Jesus prays in agony in the garden, asking that the cup pass but submitting to the Father’s will.
Judas leads a crowd with swords and clubs to arrest Jesus, and the disciples flee.

e.n: Jesus before the high priest; Peter denies him
t: Jesus is questioned by Annas and Caiaphas while Peter denies knowing him three times.
Traditional location.
Judas, seeing Jesus condemned, returns the silver and takes his own life, and the priests buy a field with the money.
Traditional site of Akeldama.
Pilate questions Jesus, finds no guilt, and finally gives him up to be crucified.
The location of the praetorium is debated.
Pilate sends Jesus to Herod, who mocks him and sends him back.
Place of Herod’s stay is not named.
Soldiers mock Jesus, and Simon of Cyrene is made to carry his cross.
Jesus is crucified between two criminals, forgives those who killed him, and dies.
Traditional site beneath the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus lay Jesus in a new tomb, and a guard is set.
Women find the tomb empty, and Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus.
The risen Jesus walks with two disciples and is recognized when he breaks bread.
Site debated; Emmaus-Qubeibeh is one candidate.

e.n: Jesus appears in the upper room
t: Jesus appears to the gathered disciples, shows them his hands and side, and opens the Scriptures to them.
Setting is a locked room; the traditional site is the Upper Room.
A week later Jesus appears to Thomas, who says, “My Lord and my God!”
The risen Jesus cooks breakfast for seven disciples on the shore and restores Peter.
Traditional spot at Tabgha.
Jesus meets the eleven on a mountain and sends them to make disciples of all nations.
Mountain not named.
Jesus blesses the disciples and is taken up into heaven.
Luke says near Bethany; Acts 1 names the Mount of Olives.

f: is, was, are, it is, will be, were

t: The Greek λέγω (legō) means “to speak.” It appears 981 times in the four Gospels, most in Matthew (292).
f: saying, i say, says, he says, he was saying, say

t: The Greek ἔπω (epō) means “to say.” It appears 763 times in the four Gospels, most in Luke (296).

t: A very common Jewish name in the first century: Greek for Yeshua, the same as Joshua, “the LORD saves.”
f: jesus, to jesus, when jesus, joshua, after jesus

t: The Greek ἄνθρωπος (anthrōpos) means “a human.” It appears 325 times in the four Gospels, most in Matthew (115).

t: Jews writing in Greek used theos for the one God of Israel, while in the wider Roman world it named any of countless gods.
A Jewish father held authority over the whole household, so calling God “Father” carried both closeness and authority.
f: father, fathers, as father, to father, the fathers, a father

t: “Son of” could mean sharing a character (“sons of thunder”). Rome also styled Caesar Augustus a “son of god,” so the phrase was loaded.
Everyday “sir” or “master,” but also the Greek Bible’s stand-in for God’s name and a title Romans used for Caesar.
f: lord, master, the lord, sir, masters, the lord’

t: A disciple lived with a teacher and copied his life as well as his words, often literally walking behind him.
The Greek ἀκούω (akouō) means “to hear.” It appears 228 times in the four Gospels, most in Luke (64).
f: having heard, hearing, to hear, heard, you have heard, he should hear

t: The Greek δίδωμι (didōmi) means “to give.” It appears 227 times in the four Gospels, most in John (75).

t: Many Jews said “heaven” to avoid speaking God’s name, which is why Matthew writes “kingdom of heaven.”

Hebrew for “save now!” from Psalm 118, shouted by pilgrims at festivals and by crowds greeting a king.

e.n: House of prayer / den of robbers
t: Jeremiah 7 used the phrase of the temple, where people shelter after their crimes. Jesus quotes it while clearing the money changers.
In a culture ranked by honor, humility meant low status, so Jesus making it a virtue was a reversal.
A hypocrite was a Greek stage actor wearing a mask, so the word means playing a part.
“I am” echoes God’s own name, which is why the arresting soldiers draw back and fall.

e.n: I am the bread of life
t: The crowd had just asked for bread from heaven like Moses’ manna, and Jesus says he is it.

e.n: I am the light of the world
t: Said around the Feast of Tabernacles, which included a lamp-lighting ceremony in the temple, so the image would have been vivid.

e.n: I am the resurrection and the life
t: Martha believed in resurrection “at the last day.” Jesus makes it a person, present now.

e.n: I am the way, the truth, and the life
t: Said to disciples about to lose him. “The Way” later became one of the earliest names for Christians (Acts 9:2).

e.n: I and the father are one
t: Said at the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah). The crowd picks up stones because they hear a claim to deity.
From Isaiah 7:14, “God with us,” a sign to King Ahaz in a political crisis that Matthew applies to Jesus.
Mark’s favorite word (euthys), used dozens of times, gives his Gospel its breathless pace.
The Passover meal was itself a remembrance of the exodus, and Jesus gives the bread and cup a new one.
The road from Jerusalem to Jericho drops over 3,000 feet through desert hills known for robbers.
Tetelestai was used for completing a task and, on receipts, for a debt paid.
Literally “I am,” echoing God’s name, spoken as Jesus walks on a sea that Job 9:8 says only God treads.
The Greek is a quiet weeping, distinct from the loud wailing of the mourners.
A courtroom word: declared righteous. The tax collector goes home declared right with God.
Night was divided into watches, so this means staying awake at your post like servants waiting for their master.
Passover lambs, the daily temple lamb and Isaiah 53’s servant “like a lamb” all stand behind this title.
Leaven was a bit of old fermented dough. The woman’s three measures of flour is a large batch, enough for a feast.
A Roman legion was several thousand soldiers, so the name draws on the occupying army’s symbol of power.
Echoes Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses promises a prophet like himself whom Israel must hear.
Living water meant fresh, flowing spring water, prized over stored cistern water.
Magi were Persian-style priest-astronomers who studied the stars. Matthew never says there were three.
A disciple was an apprentice who learned by living with the teacher; here the call extends to all nations.
Mercy translates Hebrew chesed, faithful covenant love, not merely feeling sorry.
A mina was about a hundred denarii, roughly three months’ wages for a laborer.
Mammon is Aramaic for wealth, almost personified as a rival master.

e.n: My time has not yet come
t: Kairos means the appointed moment, which John ties to God’s timing rather than the calendar.
In Daniel a “mystery” is a hidden thing God reveals. The kingdom is hidden to outsiders and revealed to disciples.
In Daniel a “mystery” is a hidden thing God reveals. The kingdom is hidden to outsiders and revealed to disciples.
Nazareth was a tiny Galilean village, so “Nazarene” was a tag of obscurity.
For many Jews “neighbor” meant fellow Israelites. The Samaritan story stretches it to include an enemy.
The Law already said to love your neighbor; the new part is “as I have loved you.” Latin mandatum gives us “Maundy” Thursday.
A covenant was a binding agreement sealed by sacrifice or a meal. Jeremiah 31 promised a new one, which Jesus announces at the Passover meal.
From Genesis 2:24. In a world where a man could easily divorce, Jesus roots marriage in creation.
Ezekiel 34 promised God would gather scattered sheep. Here Jesus includes sheep beyond Israel.
Luke writes in the style of Greek historians who dedicated careful accounts to a patron.
Used for the cloud covering the tabernacle in Exodus, so God’s presence rests on Mary.
A Persian loan word for a walled royal garden, later used for the place of the blessed.
Teleios means whole or complete rather than flawless; the picture is maturity.
Anaideia means shameless boldness. In a hospitality culture a friend knocking at midnight shames the host into helping.
The widow’s two small copper coins were the smallest in circulation.
Same root as “clean”: vinedressers cleaned and trimmed branches so they would bear more fruit.
An Aramaic, more personal form of “rabbi”: “my teacher.”
Lytron was the price paid to free a slave or prisoner of war. Jesus says his life is that price.
Used for buying back slaves or prisoners, with Israel’s Exodus as the pattern.
A denarius carried Caesar’s face and title, so the coin was his; people bear God’s image, so they belong to God.
Literally “change your mind.” The prophets’ equivalent was “turn back,” a change of direction.
Literally “change your mind.” The prophets’ equivalent was “turn back,” a change of direction.
Literally “change your mind.” The prophets’ equivalent was “turn back,” a change of direction.
Simon’s new name, Cephas in Aramaic, means rock.
Salt preserved, seasoned and sealed covenants, and it was used in temple sacrifices.
To set apart for God, as the priests, temple and Sabbath were.
Used for gods and for emperors like Augustus. Luke gives the title to a baby in a manger; John has Samaritans say it.
Used for gods and for emperors like Augustus. Luke gives the title to a baby in a manger; John has Samaritans say it.
John notes that Siloam means “sent,” the pool where the blind man was told to wash.
Diakonos meant waiting on tables, a low-status job, which Jesus takes on himself.
Echoes Lamech’s seventy-sevenfold vengeance in Genesis 4:24, reversed into forgiveness.
Shepherds were low in status, yet “shepherd” was also a title for kings and for God.
Wheat was shaken in a sieve to separate grain from chaff, and Satan asks to do that to Peter.
A messianic title; a blind man calling it out shows he sees who Jesus is.
“Son of” could mean sharing a character, and Rome styled Caesar Augustus a “son of god.”
From Daniel 7, a human figure given everlasting rule. In Aramaic it can also just mean “a human being.”
Its Aramaic name is Gabbatha, where Pilate sat in judgment; its exact location is debated.
A skandalon was the trigger of a trap, so to cause stumbling is to set a snare.
Aramaic for “little girl, get up.” Mark preserves the Aramaic words Jesus spoke.
Jewish law required two or three witnesses, which is why John lines up witnesses for Jesus.
Both “test” and “tempt.” God tests to prove faith, Satan tempts to make it fail, and the wilderness echoes Israel’s forty years.
The bottomless deep, which Jewish writing treated as a prison for evil spirits.
Greek for “Messiah,” the anointed one, a hoped-for king from David’s line.
In John “the hour” is the appointed time of Jesus’ death and glory, which he had said had not yet come.
Jerusalem was under Gentile rule, and Luke 21 uses the phrase for the period of Gentile domination.

e.n: The truth will set you free
t: Said to listeners who claimed never to have been enslaved, despite Egypt, Babylon and Rome.
A generation was about forty years in biblical thinking; “this generation” can recall the wilderness generation.

e.n: To the end of the age
t: Jews spoke of “this age” and “the age to come.”
The “traditions of the elders” were oral rules layered on the written Law, such as washing hands before meals.
Metamorphoo gives us “metamorphosis,” and Moses and Elijah, who also met God on mountains, appear with him.
With no banks, people buried valuables in the ground, so finding treasure in a field is believable.
Thlipsis literally means pressure, like grapes squeezed in a press, and was used for the hardship expected before the end.
A curtain screened the Holy of Holies, which only the high priest entered, once a year on the Day of Atonement.
Israel was often pictured as God’s vine or vineyard (Isaiah 5, Psalm 80), and Jesus claims to be the true one.
Isaiah 7:14 in Hebrew says “young woman”; the Greek translation Matthew quotes says parthenos, “virgin.”
Episkope means God coming to inspect or rescue; Luke says Jerusalem missed God’s coming.
Darnel looks like wheat until it heads out, and Roman law had penalties for sowing it in an enemy’s field.
Tithing herbs like mint and dill was careful law-keeping, and Jesus says the heavy matters are justice, mercy and faithfulness.
Combines Psalm 2:7 (the royal son) and Isaiah 42:1 (the servant).
Tombs were whitewashed so people could see them and avoid contact and uncleanness.
Farmers tossed grain in the air with a fork so the wind blew the chaff away, a ready picture of judgment.
Jewish law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter.
Mammon is Aramaic for wealth, almost personified as a rival master.
A yoke joins two animals to pull a load. Rabbis spoke of the “yoke of the Law” and the “yoke of the kingdom.”
“Zeal for your house” echoes Psalm 69, and “Zealot” later became a name for revolutionaries.

Missing the mark: failing to be what God made us to be and to do what he asks. The Gospels describe it as acts (stealing, lying, lust) and as something deeper in the heart, which is why Jesus says defilement comes from within. Jesus is called Savior because he will save his people from their sins.

Set apart, belonging to God and different from the ordinary. God is holy in a way no one else is, and people and places become holy by being set apart for him. In the Gospels, spirits cry out to Jesus as “the Holy One of God,” and Jesus teaches that holiness is about the heart as much as about ritual purity.

The Gospels use several Greek words for love, and the most important is agape: a self-giving, chosen love that wants the good of the other. Jesus says the greatest commandment is to love God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength, and the second is to love your neighbor as yourself. He tells his disciples to love one another as he has loved them, and to love even their enemies.

Unearned favor: God’s generosity toward people who cannot deserve it. John says grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Jesus’ parables of the workers in the vineyard and the prodigal son show a God who gives more than people have earned.

Trust and faithfulness. The Greek word pistis covers both believing something is true and trusting someone. Jesus often responds to faith with healing, marvels at it in a Roman soldier, and rebukes his disciples for “little faith.” The father of the boy with a spirit says, “I believe; help my unbelief.”

Letting go of a debt or offense. Jesus teaches people to ask God for forgiveness and to forgive others, forgiving “seventy times seven.” He claims the authority to forgive sins, which makes his opponents ask who can forgive sins but God alone.

A change of mind and direction, turning back to God. John the Baptist and Jesus both start by calling people to repent because the kingdom of heaven is near. The Greek word metanoia means a changed mind, and the Hebrew idea is turning around, shuv.

God’s reign and rule, already present in Jesus but not yet complete. It is Jesus’ main theme: he announces it, teaches about it in parables, and shows it with healings and exorcisms. Matthew usually says “kingdom of heaven,” which means the same thing.

Rescue and wholeness. In the Gospels the verb “to save” can mean rescued from drowning, healed of illness, or saved from sin and death. Jesus’ name means “the Lord saves.” John 3:16 says God so loved the world that he gave his Son so that everyone who believes would have eternal life.

Being in right standing with God, and living the way God desires. Jesus says that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees you will not enter the kingdom, and tells people to seek first God’s kingdom and his righteousness.

Making things right between God and humanity at the cost of a sacrifice. In the Gospels, Jesus says the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many, and at the Last Supper calls the cup his blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins. How the cross accomplishes this has been described in several ways in Christian history.

Rising bodily from death. Pharisees believed in it, Sadducees did not. Jesus teaches that he is “the resurrection and the life” and that he would be killed and rise on the third day, and all four Gospels report the empty tomb and his appearances afterward.
Life of the age to come, beginning now in knowing God. In John it means above all knowing the Father and Jesus Christ. In the other Gospels, people ask Jesus what they must do to inherit it.

God’s final putting right of all things, when everyone answers for how they lived. Jesus speaks of a day of judgment, of separating sheep and goats, and also says he did not come to judge the world but to save it. He also commands his followers not to judge hypocritically.

Jesus uses two different words usually translated hell. Gehenna, from the Valley of Hinnom just south of Jerusalem, was once a place of child sacrifice and later a rubbish dump, and became a picture of final judgment. Hades is the realm of the dead. Christians have understood what Jesus teaches about final punishment in different ways.

In the Gospels, “heaven” can mean the sky, God’s dwelling place, or a way of speaking about God himself (“kingdom of heaven”). Jesus speaks of treasure in heaven, angels in heaven, and the Father in heaven.

Speaking with God. Jesus prays alone, often early in the morning or at night, and teaches his disciples to pray simply, persistently and without showing off. He gives them the Lord’s Prayer, and in John 17 prays at length for himself, his disciples and all who will believe.

The prayer Jesus taught his disciples. Matthew gives a longer form, in the Sermon on the Mount, and Luke a shorter one when the disciples ask him to teach them to pray. It begins “Our Father in heaven” and asks for God’s name to be honored, his kingdom to come, daily bread, forgiveness and rescue from the evil one.

Going without food, usually for a spiritual purpose. Jesus fasts forty days in the wilderness, teaches that fasting should be private, and says his disciples will fast when the bridegroom is taken from them.

Immersion in water as a sign of repentance and cleansing. John the Baptist baptized for repentance, and Jesus was baptized by him in the Jordan. Jesus’ followers are told to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Christians have understood and practiced baptism in different ways.

The meal Jesus shared with his disciples the night he was betrayed, when he gave them bread and wine as his body and his blood of the new covenant. Different Christian traditions call it Communion, the Eucharist or the Mass, and understand it in different ways.

Compassion in action toward people in need or in the wrong. The Gospels often say Jesus was moved with compassion. He says, “Blessed are the merciful,” and tells the religious leaders to learn what Hosea meant: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice.”
Not thinking of oneself too highly, and taking the lowest place. Jesus says he is “gentle and lowly in heart,” washes his disciples’ feet, and says that whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

Following Jesus as a learner and apprentice. He calls people to follow him, and to take up their cross and lose their lives for his sake. The Twelve are the closest disciples, but many others follow, including women.

Jesus is blunt about money. He says, “You cannot serve God and money,” tells a rich man to sell what he has and give to the poor, blesses the poor in spirit and warns that the rich will find it hard to enter the kingdom. Luke gives special attention to the poor and the outcast.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his followers not to be anxious about food, drink and clothing, because the Father knows what they need. He points to the birds and the lilies and says, “Seek first the kingdom of God.”

Wholeness and well-being, not only the absence of conflict. The angels announce peace on earth at his birth, Jesus tells people to “go in peace,” and before his death he says, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.” After the resurrection, the first thing he says to the disciples is, “Peace be with you.”

In John, truth is not just a set of correct statements but something found in a person. Jesus says, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life,” and that the truth will set people free. Pilate asks, “What is truth?”

A word picture running through the Bible for God’s presence, truth and goodness, in contrast with darkness. John opens with the Word as the light shining in the darkness, and Jesus says, “I am the light of the world.” He also tells his followers, “You are the light of the world.”

The weighty, shining presence of God. In the Old Testament it fills the tabernacle and temple. John says the Word became flesh and “we have seen his glory.” In John, the cross is the hour when Jesus is glorified.

Honoring and adoring God. Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, and he accepts worship himself from the Magi, the man born blind and Thomas.

A testing or enticement to sin. After his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, where he fasts forty days and is tempted by Satan. Each time he answers with Scripture from Deuteronomy. In the Lord’s Prayer, his followers ask not to be led into temptation.

Acting a part. The Greek word was used for a stage actor. Jesus warns about it in prayer, giving and fasting, and in Matthew 23 pronounces seven woes on scribes and Pharisees who do not practice what they teach.

Messengers of God. Gabriel announces the births of John and Jesus, an angel appears to Joseph, and angels announce the birth to the shepherds. Angels minister to Jesus after the temptation and in Gethsemane, and they are at the empty tomb.

Evil spirits that afflict people. Jesus casts them out with a word, and they recognize who he is. The Gospels distinguish demon possession from ordinary illness, though modern readers understand the conditions described in different ways. Jesus says the exorcisms show that the kingdom of God has come.

Good news. The Greek word euangelion was used for the announcement of a king’s victory or birth. Mark opens, “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ,” and Jesus preaches “the gospel of the kingdom.” Matthew, Mark, Luke and John are each called a Gospel because each tells the good news about Jesus.

The community of Jesus’ followers. Jesus uses the word ekklesia only twice in the Gospels, both in Matthew, when he says to Peter, “On this rock I will build my church,” and when he teaches how to deal with a brother who sins. The word means an assembly or gathering.
