God’s instruction given through Moses, first the five books of the Torah and then, in a wider sense, the whole Hebrew Scriptures. Jesus says he has come to fulfill it, summarizes it as love of God and neighbor, and argues with others over how to keep it.

Asked which commandment is greatest, Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:4-5, loving the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength, and Leviticus 19:18, loving your neighbor as yourself, and says all the Law and Prophets depend on these two.

Jesus’ longest block of teaching, in Matthew 5 to 7, given on a hillside near Capernaum. It includes the Beatitudes, teaching on anger, lust, oaths and enemies, the Lord’s Prayer, the warning about worry and the call to build on the rock. Luke has a shorter parallel, often called the Sermon on the Plain.
The ordinary word for God. In Hebrew, Elohim (a plural form used with singular verbs); in Greek, theos. The Gospels use it constantly, and John 1:1 says the Word was God.

God’s personal name, revealed to Moses at the burning bush. It was considered too holy to speak, so Jews said Adonai (“Lord”) instead, and most English Bibles print LORD in capitals. In the Greek Old Testament it became kyrios, the same word applied to Jesus.

A title of honor meaning master or lord. For God it is Adonai in Hebrew. In the Gospels, kyrios is used as a polite “sir” and also as a title of divinity. Thomas’s confession, “My Lord and my God,” is the climax of John.
Jesus consistently speaks of God as Father, and prays to him as Abba, the Aramaic family word for father. It was unusual to address God so directly. He teaches the disciples to pray, “Our Father.”

At the burning bush, God told Moses his name was “I AM WHO I AM.” In John, Jesus uses “I am” in the absolute sense, as in “Before Abraham was, I am,” and the crowd picks up stones. He also makes seven “I am” statements with a picture word.
A title for God as above all other powers. It is used by Gabriel when speaking of Jesus, and by demons who recognize him.

A name God used with Abraham and the patriarchs, usually translated “God Almighty.” It stresses his power and sufficiency. The Gospels use the idea when Mary sings that “the Mighty One has done great things for me.”
Literally “LORD of armies,” a title that describes God as commander of heavenly and earthly forces. Common in the prophets, it appears in the Gospels mostly in Old Testament quotations.

Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua, a short form of Yehoshua (Joshua), meaning “the LORD saves.” The angel tells Joseph to give the child this name “because he will save his people from their sins.”

Christ is Greek (Christos) for the Hebrew Mashiach, Messiah, meaning “anointed one.” Kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil. Peter confesses, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” and Matthew opens, “the genealogy of Jesus Christ.”

In Israel, “son of God” could mean the king or the nation. In the Gospels, the heavenly voice at Jesus’ baptism and transfiguration calls him “my beloved Son,” demons call him Son of God, and John says he is the only Son who is himself God.

Jesus’ favorite title for himself, used about eighty times in the Gospels and almost never by anyone else. In Aramaic it can simply mean “a human being,” but Daniel 7 uses it for a figure who comes on the clouds and receives everlasting dominion. Jesus uses it for his earthly work, his suffering and his return in glory.
f: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (ho huios tou anthrōpou)

t: A title for the promised king from David’s line. The blind men of Jericho and the crowds at the triumphal entry call Jesus by it, and Matthew begins by calling him son of David.

John the Baptist sees Jesus coming and says, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” The title draws on the Passover lamb and on Isaiah’s suffering servant, who was led like a lamb to the slaughter.

John opens, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Logos means word, reason or message, and it carried weight in both Jewish and Greek thought.
Isaiah’s name for the promised child, meaning “God with us.” Matthew applies it to Jesus at his birth, and ends his Gospel with Jesus’ promise, “I am with you always.”

“I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.” Said in Capernaum after the feeding of the five thousand, in contrast with the manna Israel ate in the wilderness.

“I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life.” Said in the temple at the Feast of Tabernacles, when great lamps were lit, and again before healing the man born blind.
“I am the door of the sheep... If anyone enters by me, he will be saved.” A shepherd sometimes slept across the opening of the sheepfold so that he was the door.
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” The picture of God as shepherd runs through Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34.
“I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live.” Said to Martha at the tomb of Lazarus just before he raises him.

e.n: The Way, the Truth and the Life
t: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” Jesus says this to Thomas in the upper room, when the disciples ask where he is going.
“I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.” Israel was often pictured as God’s vine, and Jesus says his disciples must abide in him to bear fruit.
Jesus calls himself the bridegroom when asked why his disciples do not fast, and tells parables about waiting for the bridegroom. John the Baptist calls himself the friend of the bridegroom.

Rabbi, “my great one,” was a respectful address for a teacher. Disciples and others call Jesus Rabbi or Teacher, and Mary Magdalene calls him Rabboni. Jesus tells his followers not to seek the title for themselves.
Demons recognize Jesus with this title. Peter, speaking for the Twelve in John 6, also calls him “the Holy One of God.”
The Magi ask where the king of the Jews has been born, and Pilate asks Jesus whether he is. The sign above the cross reads, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews,” in three languages.
After the feeding of the five thousand, the crowd says, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world,” thinking of the prophet like Moses. Jesus calls himself a prophet in Nazareth.
Jesus says, “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve,” and Matthew sees him as Isaiah’s servant. He washes his disciples’ feet.
From Nazareth, where Jesus grew up. It is also a title used on the cross. Nathanael asked, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”

God’s Spirit, who fills John the Baptist, Elizabeth, Zechariah, Mary and Simeon in Luke, descends on Jesus at his baptism and is promised to the disciples. John gives the Spirit several titles: Helper (Paraclete), Spirit of truth.

The seventh day, a day of rest from work, kept from Friday sundown to Saturday sundown. It recalls God’s rest after creation and Israel’s rescue from slavery. In the Gospels, many conflicts with Jesus are about what is lawful on the Sabbath, and he says, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”

The yearly feast recalling the night God passed over Israelite homes in Egypt and freed his people. A lamb was sacrificed and eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. Pilgrims filled Jerusalem. All four Gospels place the death of Jesus at Passover, and the Last Supper is a Passover meal in Matthew, Mark and Luke.
A seven-day feast right after Passover, when no leaven (yeast) was eaten, recalling the haste of leaving Egypt. By Jesus’ day the two were treated almost as one eight-day festival.

A feast during the week of Unleavened Bread when the first sheaf of the barley harvest was brought to the priest. The Gospels place the resurrection on “the first day of the week” after Passover, and Paul later calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have died.

Fifty days after Passover, Israel celebrated the wheat harvest and (in later Jewish tradition) the giving of the law at Sinai. In Acts, the Spirit comes on the disciples on this day. Jesus does not mention it by name in the Gospels, but he promises the Spirit.

A day marked by trumpet blasts at the start of the seventh month, opening the autumn feast season and calling Israel to prepare for the Day of Atonement. Later Jewish tradition calls it Rosh Hashanah.

The holiest day of the year, when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to make atonement for himself and the nation, and the scapegoat carried sins into the wilderness. The Gospels do not describe it, but the temple curtain torn at Jesus’ death and the book of Hebrews connect it to his sacrifice.

A week-long autumn harvest feast when people lived in leafy booths to remember the wilderness years. Each day water was carried from the pool of Siloam to the altar and the temple courts were lit with great lamps. John 7 and 8 set Jesus’ teaching on living water and “the light of the world” in this feast.

An eight-day winter feast of lights commemorating the rededication of the temple in 164 BC after the Maccabean revolt. It is not in the Old Testament. John says Jesus was in Jerusalem at the Feast of Dedication, walking in Solomon’s Colonnade, when he said, “I and the Father are one.”

A joyful feast recalling how Esther and Mordecai saved the Jews from Haman’s plot. Some scholars think “a feast of the Jews” in John 5:1 could be Purim, but the Gospel does not say which feast it was.

Every seventh year the land was to rest and debts were released. Every fiftieth year, the Jubilee, slaves were freed and land returned to its family. Jesus’ first sermon at Nazareth uses Isaiah’s language of “proclaiming the year of the Lord’s favor.”
The day before the Sabbath (Friday), when food was prepared and work finished. The Gospels use it to date the crucifixion and burial, which had to be done before sundown when the Sabbath began.

e.n: The first day of the week
t: The day after the Sabbath. All four Gospels place the discovery of the empty tomb on this day, and Christians came to gather on it, calling it the Lord’s Day.
Many pious Jews fasted on Mondays and Thursdays. The Pharisee in Jesus’ parable says, “I fast twice a week.” Jesus teaches that fasting should be private and sincere, not for show.

A covenant is a solemn, binding agreement, often sealed with a sacrifice or a meal, between two parties. The Bible tells the story of God’s relationship with his people through a series of covenants, each building on the one before. The Greek word is diatheke, and the Latin word for it is testamentum, which is where “Testament” in Old and New Testament comes from.
After the flood, God promised never again to destroy the earth by flood and set the rainbow in the clouds as the sign. It was made with Noah, his descendants and every living creature.

God promised Abraham land, countless descendants and that all nations would be blessed through him. Circumcision was the sign. Luke has Mary and Zechariah both celebrate God remembering this covenant, and John the Baptist warns that being Abraham’s children is not enough.

At Mount Sinai, God gave Israel the law through Moses, beginning with the Ten Commandments, and the people agreed to obey. Moses sealed it with blood. Jesus says he has not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.
God promised David that his house, throne and kingdom would last forever and that his descendant would be God’s son. The Gospels open by tracing Jesus to David, and crowds greet him as Son of David.

Jeremiah promised a new covenant in which God would put his law in people’s hearts and forgive their sin. At the Last Supper, Jesus passes the cup and says it is the new covenant in his blood, poured out for many.

Priests descended from Aaron and offered sacrifices at the temple, and Levites assisted them with music, guarding and teaching. Zechariah was a priest. In the good Samaritan parable a priest and a Levite pass by the man on the road.

The chief priest of Israel, who alone entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement. In Jesus’ time the Romans appointed the office. Annas had held it earlier, and Caiaphas was high priest the year Jesus died.

The supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, made up of about seventy elders, priests and scribes, with the high priest presiding. It tried Jesus and sent him to Pilate. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were members.

Respected leaders from leading families who sat with the chief priests and scribes in the council, and who also led local communities. Together these three groups question Jesus’ authority and condemn him.
Another word for scribes: experts in the Law of Moses who copied, taught and applied it. A lawyer tests Jesus with the question about eternal life that leads to the good Samaritan parable.
A movement of Jewish nationalists who wanted to drive out the Romans by force. One of the Twelve, Simon, is called the Zealot.

A strict Jewish community with members living by the Dead Sea at Qumran, who produced the Dead Sea Scrolls. They are not named in the Gospels, but they help show the variety of Jewish life in Jesus’ day.
Luke records that Jesus sent out seventy (or seventy-two, depending on the manuscript) of his followers in pairs to the towns he was going to visit, to announce that the kingdom of God had come near.

Large groups of ordinary people who follow Jesus for healing and teaching. Their reactions swing from amazement to confusion, and Jesus has compassion on them because they are like sheep without a shepherd.
Everyone who was not Jewish. Jesus’ ministry is mostly to Jews, but he helps a Roman centurion, a Syrophoenician woman and others, and sends his followers to all nations.

In the Gospels, “sinners” often means people living outside what the religious leaders thought acceptable, such as tax collectors and prostitutes, rather than only people who had committed obvious wrongs. Jesus eats with them, and says he came to call sinners.

In the Bible, leprosy covers a range of serious skin diseases that made people ritually unclean and forced them to live apart. Jesus touches and heals lepers and sends them to the priests for confirmation.

Roman army officers commanding about a hundred soldiers. The Gospels show them in a good light: the centurion of Capernaum has great faith, and the centurion at the cross says, “Truly this man was the Son of God.”

The largest unit of the Roman army, about six thousand men. When Jesus asks the possessed man his name, he answers, “Legion, for we are many.” Jesus tells Peter that he could call twelve legions of angels.

The Roman official who ruled Judea. In Jesus’ time it was Pontius Pilate (AD 26-36). He lived in Caesarea on the coast but came to Jerusalem for the feasts, to keep order. Only he could order an execution.
The official who organized worship in a local synagogue. Jairus is one, and another is indignant when Jesus heals a woman on the Sabbath.
A local meeting place for prayer, Scripture reading and teaching, found in nearly every town. Jesus regularly taught in synagogues in Galilee, and he was rejected in the one in Nazareth.

In the ancient world, widows were among the most vulnerable people. Jesus shows special concern for them: he raises the widow of Nain’s son, praises the widow’s two small coins, and condemns those who devour widows’ houses.
Twelve men appointed to be with Jesus and to be sent out, matching the twelve tribes of Israel. The four lists in the New Testament differ slightly in the order and minor names.

e.u: Teachers who stressed the oral tradition
t: A lay movement that stressed purity, tithing, Sabbath-keeping and the “tradition of the elders”. They were respected among ordinary people and clashed with Jesus over Sabbath, table fellowship and authority.
A group of wealthy priestly families that controlled the Temple and accepted only the written Torah. They denied the resurrection and the existence of angels.
Professional teachers and copyists of Scripture, also called lawyers or teachers of the law. Many belonged to the Pharisees.
The ruling body in Jerusalem, made up of the high priest, senior priests, elders and scribes. It could try cases but needed Rome’s approval to carry out an execution.
Political backers of the Herod family. They are named only twice together with the Pharisees, plotting against Jesus.
Local men who bid for the right to collect tolls and customs, often for a share of the money. Hated as collaborators and extortioners, they are often grouped with “sinners” in the Gospels.

e.u: Neighbors of the Jews, kin of Israel
t: Descendants of the northern kingdom’s people, with their own temple on Mount Gerizim and their own Torah. Jews and Samaritans were bitter rivals, which is why Jesus’ parable of the Good Samaritan startled his listeners.

Rome ruled Judea through a prefect and auxiliary troops stationed in Caesarea and in Jerusalem’s Antonia fortress. Soldiers appear as the centurion, the Gethsemane arrest party, the mocking guard and those who cast lots for the clothing.
Hired and family shepherds who lived outdoors near Bethlehem and across Judea and Galilee. In Luke, they are the first to hear the birth announcement.

Learned men from the east, likely astrologers from Persia or Babylon, who followed a star to Jerusalem and then to Bethlehem with gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh. Matthew does not give a number.
Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna among the women who funded Jesus’ ministry. They were present at the crucifixion and discovered the empty tomb.
The Spirit descends on Jesus at his baptism and leads him into the wilderness. In John, Jesus promises the Spirit as a Helper who will teach the disciples and remind them of all he has said.
Mark and Matthew name four brothers and mention sisters. The Gospels say they did not believe in him during his ministry. James later led the Jerusalem church.

Leaven is yeast, a small piece of fermented dough that makes a whole batch rise. Jesus uses it twice: as a warning, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees,” meaning their hypocrisy and teaching, and as a picture of the kingdom of God spreading quietly through the world. The disciples at first thought he was talking about bread.
A Roman silver coin, about a day’s wage for a laborer or soldier. It is the pay in the workers in the vineyard parable, and Jesus asks to see one when asked about taxes to Caesar.
The smallest Greek bronze coin, worth a fraction of a denarius. The widow in the temple gives two of them, and Jesus says she has given more than all the rest.

A very large unit of weight, about 75 pounds (34 kg), used for silver and gold. A single talent was worth about fifteen years of a laborer’s wages. In the parable of the talents, the servants receive five, two and one.
A Greek unit worth about a hundred denarii, or about three months’ wages. In Luke’s parable of the minas, the servants each receive one.

A silver shekel was the Jewish temple coin. The stater was a Greek silver coin worth four drachmas, the exact temple tax for two people. Jesus tells Peter that the coin in the fish’s mouth will be enough for both of them.

The price Judas was paid to betray Jesus. It was also the compensation for a slave gored by an ox in the law of Moses. Judas threw the coins into the temple and the priests used them to buy the potter’s field.
The staple food, usually barley or wheat flatbread baked daily. Jesus feeds crowds with it, calls himself the bread of life, and breaks it at the Last Supper and on the road to Emmaus.
A main source of protein in Galilee, usually dried or pickled. Several of the disciples were fishermen. Fish appear in the feedings, the miraculous catches and the breakfast on the beach.
The ordinary drink at meals, usually mixed with water. Jesus makes water into wine at Cana, is accused of being “a drunkard,” and uses the cup of wine at the Last Supper.
A bag made from animal skin that held wine. New wine ferments and expands, so it needs flexible new skins. Old, stiff skins would burst.
The cup of wine at the Passover meal, which Jesus calls the new covenant in his blood. It also stands for suffering: in Gethsemane he prays, “Let this cup pass from me.”

Six large stone jars, each holding twenty to thirty gallons, used for Jewish rites of purification. Stone did not become ceremonially unclean like pottery. Jesus has them filled with water, which becomes wine.

A small clay lamp burning olive oil, which gave a dim light. It was put on a stand, not under a basket. Jesus says, “You are the light of the world,” and lamps feature in the parable of the ten virgins.

A tiny seed, proverbially the smallest a farmer sowed, that grows into a bush two to three meters tall. Jesus compares the kingdom of God to it, and says faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains.

A heavy grinding stone. A large one turned by a donkey was far heavier than the small hand mills women used each morning. Jesus says it would be better to be thrown into the sea with a millstone around the neck than to cause a little one to stumble.

A wooden beam that joined two animals for plowing. Rabbis spoke of the “yoke of the law” and a teacher’s yoke. Jesus invites the weary, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me... for my yoke is easy.”

Leather soles tied to the foot with straps. Taking off or carrying another’s sandals was a servant’s task. John the Baptist says he is not worthy to untie the thong of the coming one’s sandals. Disciples are told to take no extra pair.

The tunic was the basic undergarment, and the cloak a heavier outer garment that also served as a blanket. The law forbade keeping a poor person’s cloak overnight. Jesus says that if someone takes your tunic, give your cloak as well.

Jewish men wore tassels on the corners of their cloaks to remember God’s commandments. The woman with a hemorrhage touches Jesus’ tassel, and Jesus criticizes the scribes who lengthen theirs for show.
Small leather boxes containing Scripture verses, strapped to the forehead and arm during prayer. Jesus criticizes those who make their phylacteries broad to be noticed.

A small flask carved from soft stone, used for expensive perfume. A woman breaks one and pours nard on Jesus’ head or feet. John names her as Mary of Bethany and says the perfume was worth about a year’s wages.

The gifts of the Magi. Gold was for kings, frankincense was incense used in temple worship, and myrrh was a fragrant resin used in burial. Matthew does not say there were three Magi, only three gifts.
Strips of cloth wrapped around a newborn to keep it warm and still. Luke gives them as a sign to the shepherds.
A feeding trough for animals, where Mary laid Jesus. Houses in Judea often kept animals in a lower room or a nearby cave. Luke does not say “stable” or “innkeeper.” The “inn” may be a guest room.
A cast net was thrown by hand and a dragnet was pulled between boats. Peter, Andrew, James and John mended and cast nets, and Jesus calls them to “fish for people.”

A wooden fishing boat. In 1986, a first-century boat was found in the mud of the Sea of Galilee, about 27 feet long, large enough for a crew of five. Jesus often teaches from a boat and crosses the lake in one.
Salt was used to season and to preserve food and it was valuable. Jesus says, “You are the salt of the earth,” and warns that salt which has lost its taste is good for nothing.
Grapevines grew throughout Judea and Galilee. Israel is called God’s vine in the prophets, and Jesus says, “I am the true vine.”
A common tree whose fruit was eaten fresh, dried or pressed into cakes. Jesus uses it in parables about fruitfulness and readiness, and Nathanael was under a fig tree when Jesus saw him.

The most important animal in Israel’s economy and a constant image in the Gospels, for people in need, followers of Jesus and God’s flock. Shepherds lived with their flocks, so the title “shepherd” was personal.
A bird of the poor. Mary and Joseph offered two doves at the presentation of Jesus, and doves were sold in the temple courts. The Spirit descends “like a dove” at Jesus’ baptism.
Guests in a house had their dusty feet washed by a servant. At the Last Supper, Jesus takes off his outer garment, wraps a towel around his waist and washes his disciples’ feet.

A fire of burning charcoal appears twice in John: in the high priest’s courtyard where Peter warms himself and denies Jesus, and on the beach where the risen Jesus cooks fish for breakfast and later restores Peter.
A wreath of thorny branches that Roman soldiers pressed on Jesus’ head to mock him as a king, together with a purple robe and a reed for a scepter.

A Roman method of execution for slaves, rebels and non-citizens, designed to be slow and humiliating. The condemned usually carried the crossbeam to the place of execution. Jesus tells his followers to take up their own cross.
A sign (titulus) stating the charge. John says Pilate had it written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” The chief priests asked him to change it, and he refused.
A Roman soldier pierced Jesus’ side with a spear to confirm that he was dead, and blood and water came out. John sees this as fulfilling Scripture.

A small bushy herb used to sprinkle blood and water in purification rituals, and at the first Passover to apply lamb’s blood to doorposts. John says a sponge of sour wine was lifted to Jesus’ lips on a hyssop branch.

Jews wrapped bodies in linen strips with spices such as myrrh and aloes. Nicodemus brought about seventy-five pounds of them for Jesus’ burial. Peter and John later see the empty linen cloths and the face cloth folded separately.

Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, which was either wedged in place or rolled in a groove across the entrance. Joseph of Arimathea laid Jesus in his own new tomb, cut from rock, and the women find the stone rolled away.
Books were scrolls of parchment or papyrus. In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus is handed the scroll of Isaiah, finds the place and reads.

Roman soldiers and the temple guard were armed. In Gethsemane, a disciple draws a sword and cuts off a servant’s ear, and Jesus says, “Put your sword back... for all who take the sword will perish by the sword.”

A rule of later Jewish tradition limiting how far one could walk on the Sabbath, about 2,000 cubits (about three-quarters of a mile). Luke mentions it when describing the distance from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem.

Franciscan archaeologists (from 1968) dug under an octagonal church and found a cluster of small basalt houses around shared courtyards. One room was plastered and used for gatherings from the 1st century on, and later got a church of its own.
The Gospels place Jesus’ base, and Simon Peter’s home, in Capernaum. The early veneration of this one house, and the way it changed from a home into a meeting place, makes it a strong candidate.
Caution: No inscription names Peter. The link rests on early veneration, not on a signed doorway.
f: Capernaum, north shore of the Sea of Galilee
1st century AD, with a church built over it in the 5th

e.n: Capernaum: the white synagogue and the black one beneath
t: The striking white limestone synagogue visible today is later than Jesus. Beneath it, excavators found black basalt walls and a pavement that many think belonged to a 1st-century synagogue.
Luke says a Roman centurion helped build the town’s synagogue, and Mark and Luke show Jesus teaching and healing there on the Sabbath. The basalt layer is the likeliest remnant of that building.
Caution: The white building you see is 300+ years after Jesus; scholars still argue about its exact date and about the basalt layer.
f: White building 4th–5th century AD; basalt foundations below are earlier

t: In the drought of 1986 two brothers spotted the outline of a wooden hull in the exposed mud. It is about 27 ft (8.2 m) long and 7.5 ft (2.3 m) wide, patched with at least a dozen kinds of wood, and could hold around 15 people. Radiocarbon and pottery date it to Jesus’ time.

It shows the kind of working fishing boat the Gospels describe: a vessel big enough to carry a teacher and a few disciples, to be rowed or sailed across the lake, or to serve as a floating platform near the shore.
Caution: The nickname is modern. Nothing links this boat to Jesus or his disciples; it is evidence of the same world.

e.n: Fishing on the lake: hooks, weights and salted fish
t: Lead weights for casting nets, stone anchors and bronze fishhooks turn up at lakeshore sites such as Magdala and Bethsaida. Magdala’s Greek name, Taricheae, means “salted fish”, and it was a processing center for the catch.
It was a real trade with owners, hired men and partners, as Zebedee and his sons show. Fishing also fed the economy that taxes and tolls were collected from along the shore.

e.n: Magdala: a synagogue with a carved stone
t: Excavations since 2009 uncovered a 1st-century synagogue, a market, harbor installations and ritual baths. In the synagogue hall lay the Magdala Stone, carved with a seven-branched menorah and other Temple symbols.
Magdala was the home of Mary Magdalene. The synagogue is one of the very few from Jesus’ lifetime, and the stone suggests how closely Galilean Jews felt tied to the Jerusalem Temple.
Caution: The Gospels never say Jesus taught in Magdala’s synagogue; it shows the setting, not a recorded event.
f: Magdala (Migdal), west shore of the lake
1st century BC – AD 67 (the town was destroyed in the revolt)

t: A Byzantine church floor in front of the altar shows a basket of loaves flanked by two fish. Nearby springs flowed into the lake, the “seven springs” (Heptapegon) that gave the place its Arabic name.
Pilgrims since the 4th century have remembered the feeding of the crowd here, and the nearby shoreline chapel recalls the breakfast on the beach after the resurrection.
Caution: The Gospels do not name the exact spot, and John places the feeding near Bethsaida; Tabgha is the traditional site.
f: Mosaic about AD 450–480 (church tradition from the 4th century)

e.n: Chorazin: a town of black basalt
t: Excavations show a basalt town with houses, olive presses and ritual baths. Its later synagogue is richly carved and held a basalt “Seat of Moses” for the one reading the Law.

Jesus names Chorazin with Bethsaida and Capernaum as towns that saw his miracles and did not repent, yet the Gospels record none of those miracles. The town shows how much of his work we do not read about.
Caution: The impressive synagogue is later than Jesus, though a 1st-century settlement lay beneath it.
f: Town of Jesus’ day; ornate synagogue 3rd–4th century AD

e.n: Bethsaida: et-Tell and a rival site
t: At et-Tell, excavators found an Iron Age city gate, and Hellenistic and Roman houses, including a so-called fisherman’s house with hooks and net weights. A second candidate, el-Araj, nearer the shore, has been dug since 2015.
Bethsaida was the hometown of Peter, Andrew and Philip, and the place where Jesus healed a blind man by stages and (by Luke) fed the five thousand nearby.
Caution: Which mound is the true Bethsaida is still debated.
f: North shore of the lake, east of the Jordan
1st century AD (city of Philip the tetrarch)

t: A large cave and a strong spring pour out at the foot of Mount Hermon. Beside them are niches carved for the god Pan and the nymphs, and the footings of a temple Herod built for Augustus. Philip the tetrarch renamed the city Caesarea.

Jesus asks his disciples “Who do people say that I am?” in the district around this pagan city. Some scholars suggest the cave, regarded as a gate to the underworld, forms the backdrop for “the gates of Hades.”
Caution: The Gospels never describe the shrine; the connection to “gates of Hades” is a suggestion, not a statement.
f: Shrine of Pan from the 3rd century BC; Philip’s city from 2 BC

e.n: The east shore: Kursi, Gadara and Hippos
t: Kursi, on the steep eastern shore, has a large Byzantine monastery and church that, by tradition, mark the healing of the demoniac. Gadara (Umm Qais) kept a theater and colonnaded street, and Hippos (Sussita) a hilltop forum and church.

This was Gentile country, the Decapolis, where pigs were raised. Matthew, Mark and Luke use different names for the district (Gadarenes, Gerasenes), which tells us the story’s location was already being remembered in several ways.
Caution: Kursi is the traditional site only; Gadara and Gerasa are inland, and the Gospels’ own names differ.
f: Sea of Galilee’s east shore and the Decapolis
Roman Decapolis cities; Byzantine monastery at Kursi

e.n: Tiberias and Sepphoris: Herod Antipas’s new cities
t: Antipas rebuilt Sepphoris, about 6 km (under 4 miles) from Nazareth, as a showpiece capital with a theater, and founded Tiberias on the lake. Excavations show Roman-style streets, public baths and prosperous houses.

Jesus grew up between these projects. The Gospels never say he entered either city, though the lake bears the name “Sea of Tiberias” in John, and Antipas, the city’s founder, appears in the story of John the Baptist.
Caution: The Gospels do not mention a visit to either city; the possibility that Jesus worked there as a builder is a scholar’s guess.
f: Sepphoris rebuilt after 4 BC; Tiberias founded AD 18–20

t: Digs under and around modern Nazareth reveal a small farming village: cisterns, grain silos, wine and olive presses and rock-cut tombs. A 1st-century house was found beside the Church of the Annunciation, and “Nazareth Village” is a modern reconstruction on an excavated farm.

This is the setting of Jesus’ childhood and the synagogue scene in Luke 4. The finds confirm a modest place with a few dozen households, matching Nathanael’s question, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”
Caution: Nazareth Village is a reconstruction, and the grotto under the Church of the Annunciation is venerated, not proved.
f: Village of the 1st century BC – 1st century AD

t: Khirbet Qana, a ruin about 14 km north of Nazareth, has Roman-era houses, tombs, and later pilgrim sites. Kafr Kanna, the modern village nearer to Nazareth, hosts the traditional Wedding Church.
Two signs happen at Cana in John’s Gospel: the water into wine and the healing of an official’s son. Which village it was affects the route Jesus took.
Caution: Some scholars prefer Khirbet Qana (older name, early pilgrim reports); Kafr Kanna has the longer pilgrim tradition. No inscription settles it.

A rounded mountain rising out of the Jezreel Valley, crowned by a Franciscan basilica (1924) and a Greek Orthodox church. Josephus says he fortified the summit in AD 66, so it was a military site in the lifetime of the first Christians.
Christians from the 4th century on have honored Tabor as the mountain of the Transfiguration, though the Gospels simply say “a high mountain”.
Caution: An alternate site is Mount Hermon, nearer to Caesarea Philippi. The Gospels give no name.
f: Fortified in the 1st century; churches from the 4th–6th centuries

t: A hill above the lake with a small octagonal church (1938) and a broad natural slope that works like an amphitheater. The pilgrim Egeria in the 4th century mentions a cave and a hillside nearby that were honored in memory of the sermon.
Matthew places Jesus’ great sermon “on the mountain”; Luke says “on a level place.” Neither names the spot, but the lakeshore slopes make it easy to see how a large crowd could hear one voice.
Caution: The site is traditional. The Gospels don’t say where the sermon was given.
f: Church built 1938; tradition from the 4th century

e.n: Synagogues of Jesus’ day: Gamla, Magdala and the Theodotus stone
t: Gamla, a town on the Golan destroyed by Rome in AD 67, preserved a basalt synagogue with stone benches around the walls. In Jerusalem, a Greek inscription (the Theodotus stone) records a synagogue built “for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments,” with a guesthouse for travelers.
The Gospels picture Jesus reading and teaching in synagogues. These buildings show they were community halls as much as places of worship: meeting rooms, schools and hostels.
Caution: Few synagogues from before AD 70 survive, so scholars debate exactly how they were used.

e.n: Qumran and the Dead Sea Scrolls
t: Between 1947 and 1956 shepherds and archaeologists found hundreds of scrolls in eleven caves above a desert settlement. The settlement has stepped, plastered pools used for ritual washing and a long communal dining room.

The community saw itself as the voice “crying in the wilderness” of Isaiah 40:3, the same verse the Gospels apply to John the Baptist. It shows that waiting for God’s coming in the Judean desert and ritual immersion were part of Jewish life in Jesus’ day.
Caution: There is no evidence that John or Jesus visited Qumran. The scrolls are background, not a record of the Gospel events.
f: Northwest shore of the Dead Sea
Settlement 2nd century BC – AD 68; scrolls about 250 BC – AD 68

t: A nearly complete scroll of Isaiah, about 7.3 m (24 ft) long, sewn from 17 sheets of parchment. It was found in 1947 and is the oldest copy of the whole book of Isaiah by over a thousand years.
In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus is handed the scroll of Isaiah and finds the passage about the Lord’s anointed. This is what such a scroll looked like and how it was unrolled.
Caution: It is a Dead Sea scroll, not the one Jesus held, but a copy of the same text from his world.
f: Found in Qumran Cave 1; kept at the Israel Museum, Jerusalem

e.n: Al-Maghtas and Qasr al-Yahud: where John baptized
t: On the east bank (Jordan), a UNESCO site has pools, baptism steps and several churches, with “Elijah’s Hill” nearby. On the west bank, across the river, Qasr al-Yahud has its own monasteries. Pilgrims from the 4th century, and the 6th-century Madaba mosaic map, mark this stretch.
John 1:28 says John baptized at “Bethany beyond the Jordan,” which fits the east bank. The two sites stand opposite each other.
Caution: Both banks honor the baptism; no inscription names the spot.
f: Lower Jordan River, east and west banks
Byzantine churches 5th–6th century; tradition from the 4th century

t: A steep desert cliff above Jericho with caves where hermits lived from the early Byzantine period. A Greek Orthodox monastery clings to the rock face.
Christians have long linked this wilderness to the forty days Jesus fasted. The name Quarantal comes from the Latin for “forty”.
Caution: The Gospels say only “the wilderness”. The identification is traditional.
f: Hermits from the 4th century; Orthodox monastery 1895

t: A fortress-palace on a lonely ridge, with a bath, a dining hall and cells cut in the rock. Italian and Hungarian digs have exposed its rooms and the Roman siege ramp from AD 72.
The Jewish historian Josephus says John the Baptist was imprisoned and killed here by Herod Antipas. The Gospels give the banquet and the beheading but never name the place.
Caution: The location comes from Josephus, not the Gospels.
f: Rebuilt by Herod the Great, in use in Jesus’ day

e.n: Herodium: the fortress-palace of Herod the Great
t: An artificial cone-shaped hill with a circular palace, a theater with a royal box and, in 2007, the discovery of what its excavator, Ehud Netzer, believed was Herod’s tomb. Floors with mosaics and wall plaster survive in the palace.

Herod’s paranoid rule frames the birth narrative: Matthew pictures him searching for the child king. The Herodium shows the wealth and defensive mindset of the ruler who died here in 4 BC (his burial there is described by Josephus).
Caution: The Gospels never mention Herodium; it illustrates the world around the story.

e.n: Jericho: three cities in one valley
t: Tell es-Sultan, Old Testament Jericho, is among the oldest cities known. The New Testament city lay a mile or two south, where Hasmonean and Herodian kings built winter palaces with pools, gardens and diamond-patterned stonework. Herod died here in 4 BC.

Jesus passes through the oasis on his last journey up to Jerusalem, healing blind Bartimaeus on the way out and dining with Zacchaeus the chief tax collector, a man whose wealth fits the toll-rich palace town.
Caution: The Gospels’ Jericho is the Herodian oasis, not the mound of Joshua.
f: Herod’s palaces 1st century BC–AD 1; Old Testament Jericho thousands of years earlier

t: About 27 km (17 miles) of road drops from Jerusalem at roughly 750 m above sea level to Jericho more than 250 m below it. Parts of the Roman road, milestones and a ruined inn (Khan al-Hatrura, later Ottoman) survive in the Wadi Qelt.
The Good Samaritan is set on this road: steep, remote, ideal for ambush. Jesus’ audience would have known exactly how dangerous it was.
Caution: The “Inn of the Good Samaritan” is a later building on the traditional site; the parable is a story, not a place report.
f: Wadi Qelt and the desert descent

e.n: The Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem
t: Constantine’s basilica was built over a cave honored as the birthplace, then rebuilt in the 6th century. In 1934 excavators uncovered a beautiful mosaic floor under the nave from the original church. Justin Martyr, around AD 160, already speaks of a cave in Bethlehem.
Luke 2 and Matthew 2 place Jesus’ birth in Bethlehem. The unbroken veneration of this one cave from the 2nd century is among the oldest Christian site traditions.
Caution: The Gospels do not mention a cave; some homes then used caves for animals, which is how the tradition took shape.
f: Built about AD 327–339; rebuilt in the 6th century

t: East of Bethlehem, Byzantine ruins and cave-chapels mark the traditional field of the shepherds. Across the Judean hills, low stone walls and rock-cut enclosures are still used as night folds for sheep.
Luke has shepherds first to hear the birth; Jesus later calls himself the good shepherd who knows his sheep, enters through the gate and lays down his life.
Caution: Several villages claim the shepherds’ field. The Gospel does not locate it.
f: Byzantine monastery remains; folds in use since antiquity

e.n: Old Cairo: the Holy Family’s tradition
t: In the district of Old Cairo, a Roman fortress called Babylon still has a surviving tower. Coptic churches, including the Church of St. Sergius, stand over a crypt traditionally said to be where the Holy Family sheltered.
Matthew says Joseph took Mary and the child to Egypt to flee Herod. Egypt had a large Jewish community, centered on Alexandria, so refuge there made sense.
Caution: The Gospel names no place in Egypt. The fortress itself is later than Jesus’ day.
f: Roman fortress of Babylon (2nd–4th century); church traditions from the 5th century on

t: A village in the hills with two churches: the Church of the Visitation (1955) and St. John the Baptist, built on Byzantine and Crusader remains, marking where Elizabeth and Zechariah lived.
Luke says Mary travelled “into the hill country of Judea” to visit Elizabeth. The village has been honored as their home since the Byzantine centuries.
Caution: Luke names no village. Ein Karem’s link is traditional.
f: Byzantine and Crusader churches; modern churches from 1885 and 1955

e.n: The Tel Dan Stele: the “House of David”
t: In 1993–94 archaeologists found fragments of an Aramaic victory inscription carved into basalt. One line names the “House of David” and the “king of Israel”. It is the earliest known reference to David’s dynasty outside the Bible.
Matthew opens with “the son of David” and Luke ties Jesus’ birth to David’s town. The stele shows that David’s dynasty was known to Israel’s neighbors centuries before Jesus.
Caution: The text is fragmentary, and scholars still debate its wording and which king wrote it.

e.n: The Temple Mount and the Western Wall
t: Herod doubled the size of the platform to about 36 acres (14.4 hectares), faced it with enormous cut stones (some 13 m long, hundreds of tons), and added stairways, shops and gates. The lower courses of the Western Wall are Herod’s work. Broad stairs rise to the sealed Huldah Gates on the south.
This is the temple Jesus entered, taught in and predicted would fall. John records that it had been under construction for “forty-six years”, a timeline that fits Herod’s building campaign.
Caution: Nothing of the temple building itself survives; what remains is the platform around it.
f: Herod’s rebuilding began about 20–19 BC; destroyed AD 70

t: At the foot of the Western Wall, archaeologists found Herodian paving covered by massive stones hurled down by Roman soldiers in AD 70. One fallen block, carved “to the place of trumpeting”, once marked a spot where a priest sounded the Sabbath trumpet.
Jesus told his disciples that not one stone would be left on another. The rubble lies exactly as it fell, still on the street where Jesus’ contemporaries once walked.
f: South-west corner of the Temple Mount

t: A limestone block carved in Greek warns any foreigner not to pass beyond the barrier around the inner courts on penalty of death. It was found in 1871, and a second fragment was found in 1935. The first is in Istanbul, the second in Jerusalem.
The Jewish historian Josephus described this stone barrier. Jesus drove the traders out of the outer court, the Court of the Gentiles, the only part non-Jews could enter.

e.n: The Tyrian shekel and the Temple tax
t: The Temple tax had to be paid in Tyrian silver (a heavy, pure coin stamped with Melqart and an eagle). Money changers set up in the Temple courts to exchange common currency for it, and thousands of these coins turn up in Jerusalem.
This explains the money changers whose tables Jesus overturned, and the “shekel” Peter finds in the fish’s mouth to pay the tax for both of them.

Tiny bronze coins, weighing a gram or two, were minted by the Hasmonean kings and found in huge numbers in Judea. In Greek they are lepta, “thin ones”; Mark says two of them make a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin.
The poor widow dropped in two lepta, perhaps the smallest coins in circulation, and Jesus said she gave more than all the rich donors.

e.n: The denarius: the tribute penny and the day’s wage
t: The silver denarius of Tiberius shows the emperor’s head with the words “Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus”. It was the coin of a soldier’s pay and a laborer’s day. Greek silver drachmas were roughly equal in value.

When opponents asked about paying taxes to Caesar, Jesus asked for a coin and “whose image and inscription is this?” The same coin is the “denarius” of the workers in the vineyard and the lost drachma in Luke 15.

e.n: The Pilate Stone and Pilate’s coins
t: In 1961, Italian archaeologists at Caesarea’s theater found a carved block with a Latin dedication naming “Pontius Pilatus, prefect of Judea”. It is the only inscription from his lifetime naming him. Bronze coins he issued with pagan cult symbols still turn up.
It confirms Pilate as a real governor, with the title prefect, and Caesarea as the Roman capital where he lived. The Gospels move him between Caesarea and Jerusalem at Passover.
Caution: The original is in the Israel Museum; Caesarea displays a copy.
In 1990 construction work uncovered a burial cave with twelve ossuaries. Two bear the name “Joseph son of Caiaphas” and one, richly decorated, held the bones of a man of about sixty.
Josephus calls the high priest “Joseph, who was called Caiaphas”. If this is his tomb, it is the closest we get to the man who presided over the interrogation of Jesus.
Caution: Most scholars accept the identification, but some doubt it.

e.n: St Peter in Gallicantu and the high priest’s house
t: A church on the slope of Mount Zion stands over rock-cut rooms, cisterns and a pit-like prison cell. Nearby is an ancient stepped street, often dated to the 1st century, linking the lower city to Mount Zion.
Pilgrims from the Byzantine period honored this as the house of Caiaphas, where Jesus was questioned and Peter denied him before the rooster crowed.
Caution: The wealthy mansions excavated in the Upper City are better candidates for a high priest’s house. This one is a tradition.
f: Church from 1931; site tradition from the 5th century

e.n: The mansions of the Upper City and the Burnt House
t: Digs in the Upper City found grand houses with mosaics, painted plaster, stone tables, ritual baths and private courtyards. In the “Burnt House”, charred wood, a spear and a weight inscribed “of Bar Kathros” show the fire of AD 70.
This is where the priestly families lived. John describes the high priest’s courtyard, a fire in it, a doorkeeper and Peter warming his hands, details that fit a mansion of this kind.
In 2004, while repairing a sewer pipe, workers uncovered a large stepped pool with three tiers of stairs. Coins and pottery date it to the Second Temple period. It was fed by Hezekiah’s Tunnel.

In John 9 Jesus sends a blind man to wash in the pool, and John adds the meaning of its name (“Sent”). It was also the starting point of the water ceremony in the feast of Tabernacles that frames John 7.
Caution: A later Byzantine pool, further downstream, was long mistaken for the one in John.

A water tunnel, 533 m (1,750 ft) long, cut through solid rock from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam. An inscription found in the tunnel, in ancient Hebrew, records the moment the two teams dug toward each other and met. You can still wade through it.
The tunnel brought water to the Pool of Siloam, the pool where Jesus sent the blind man, and it supplied the water used at Tabernacles.
Caution: The tunnel is 700 years older than Jesus. It matters for what it fed.
f: Jerusalem, from the Gihon Spring to Siloam

e.n: The Pilgrim Road from Siloam to the Temple
t: A stepped, paved street about 600 m long ran from the Pool of Siloam up toward the Temple, with shops and drains along the way. Coins found under its pavement suggest it was built about AD 30.
This is the street pilgrims took when they came for the festivals; Jesus and the Twelve would have walked it with the crowds.
Caution: The date comes from a limited number of coins and is not accepted by everyone.
f: City of David and the Temple Mount

t: Two huge pools lay side by side, separated by a rock wall, with colonnades on all four sides and on the dividing wall, five porticoes in all. Later a Roman healing shrine (an Asklepieion) was built beside them.
John 5 begins with “a pool in Jerusalem, near the Sheep Gate, called Bethesda, which has five porticoes”. The discovery matches the detail, one of the Gospel’s most exact descriptions.
Caution: The healing shrine was added after Jesus’ time.
f: North of the Temple Mount, near the Sheep Gate
Hasmonean–Herodian pools; Roman healing shrine 2nd century AD

e.n: A scale model of Jerusalem in Jesus’ day
t: A 1:50 scale model of Jerusalem at its height just before AD 70, built from excavations and from the descriptions of Josephus, shows the walls, the Temple, Herod’s palace and the theater.
It is useful for seeing how the places in the Gospels fit together: the Temple, the Antonia, Herod’s palace, the pools and the garden east of the city.
Caution: It is a reconstruction. New digs keep changing details.
Large paving stones, some scratched with gaming boards, lie under the Sisters of Zion convent. They were long said to be the courtyard where Pilate judged Jesus.
John 19:13 says Pilate sat “at a place called the Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha”. The pavement is among the sites visited on the Via Dolorosa.
Caution: Most archaeologists date this pavement to the time of Hadrian, a century after Jesus. John names a real place, but this particular pavement is a later work.
f: Pavement from about AD 135; traditional since the Middle Ages

t: At the Citadel by the Jaffa Gate, the base of one of Herod’s three towers and parts of his palace walls survive. The palace stood in the city’s highest part and became the governor’s residence in Jerusalem.
Many scholars think Pilate judged Jesus at this palace, not at the Antonia fortress. Josephus and Philo say the governors stayed there when in Jerusalem.
Caution: The location of the trial is a scholarly argument: Herod’s palace or the Antonia fortress.

e.n: The Mount of Olives and the road from Bethphage
t: A long ridge east of the city, its slope covered by about 150,000 Jewish graves, some from Jesus’ own time. Chapels mark the Lord’s Prayer, the weeping over Jerusalem (Dominus Flevit, where first-century tombs were found) and the Ascension.
The road from Bethphage, over the summit and down into the Kidron Valley, is Jesus’ route on Palm Sunday. From here you look straight across to the Temple Mount, where he predicts its fall.
Caution: Individual chapels are traditional; the mountain itself is exactly as described.
f: Cemetery in use from the First Temple period; churches from the 4th century

t: The Aramaic name means “oil press”. A modern church stands over the rock honored as the place of Jesus’ prayer, and ancient olive trees in the garden are among the oldest in the region. A nearby cave with an olive press and cisterns is also venerated.
All four Gospels set Jesus’ arrest in an olive garden across the Kidron, just east of the city. The name fits both the trees and the oil presses that processed their harvest.
Caution: Studies date the oldest trees to about 900 years, and Rome cut down the trees around Jerusalem in AD 70.
f: Foot of the Mount of Olives
Church of All Nations 1924, over a 4th-century church

e.n: The Cenacle: the traditional Upper Room
t: A Gothic hall on Mount Zion, built by the Crusaders over earlier churches that go back to the 4th century. Below it is a shrine long venerated as the tomb of David.

Mount Zion has been remembered as the place of the Last Supper and Pentecost since the early church. The Gospels say only that Jesus sent two disciples to prepare “a large upper room, furnished and ready”.
Caution: The room you visit is medieval. A first-century upper room could have stood near here, but no evidence confirms it.
f: Crusader hall (about 12th–14th century) over a 4th-century church

e.n: The tombs of the Kidron Valley
t: Along the valley between the city and the Mount of Olives stand monumental rock-cut tombs with names such as Absalom’s Pillar, the Tomb of Zechariah and the Tomb of Bnei Hezir, the last carrying an inscription naming priests of the Hezir family.
Jesus denounces scribes who “build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the graves of the righteous.” These tombs are exactly that kind of memorial, and Jesus crossed this valley to Gethsemane.
Caution: The traditional names (Absalom, Zechariah) are later labels; they are not the original owners.

The steep Hinnom Valley wraps around the south of the old city. On its far slope are many first-century rock tombs and the Greek Orthodox Monastery of St. Onuphrius, built on the traditional “Field of Blood”.
Jesus uses the Hinnom Valley (Gehenna) as an image of judgement. Matthew says the chief priests bought a potter’s field with Judas’s returned silver and called it the Field of Blood.
Caution: The spot is traditional. Gehenna is an image drawn from the valley’s history.

e.n: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre
t: Constantine’s builders cut away a hillside to expose a tomb identified by the local Christian community, and built a church around it. Under the church are first-century burial caves, and the 2016 renovation of the shrine briefly exposed the original rock bench of the tomb.
John says Jesus was crucified “near the city”, in a garden with a new tomb. This site was a quarry outside the city wall in Jesus’ day, later turned into tombs, which matches the Gospel details.
Caution: Many scholars find it plausible, but there is no inscription naming the tomb. The case rests on early local memory.
f: First-century quarry and tombs; church begun about AD 326

t: A peaceful garden with a rock-cut tomb north of the Old City. It was popularized as Jesus’ tomb in the 19th century and remains a place of prayer for many Protestants.
It offers a picture of what a garden tomb looked like, with a rock-cut chamber, a low entrance and a long groove in front (its original purpose is debated).
Caution: Most archaeologists date the tomb to the Old Testament period, so it cannot be Jesus’ tomb.
f: Tomb cut in the Iron Age (about 8th–7th century BC); identification from 1883

e.n: Rolling-stone tombs of the Herodian period
t: Some wealthy tombs around Jerusalem, among them Herod’s Family Tomb and the Tomb of the Kings, were sealed with a great round stone that rolled in a groove across the entrance. Most burial caves were closed with a square block.

The Gospels say a great stone was rolled to close Jesus’ tomb and rolled away at Easter. These tombs show what that looked like and that such a tomb belonged to someone of means (Joseph of Arimathea was rich).
Caution: The Gospels say “rolled”, but don’t describe a disc; a square stone can also be rolled.

For about a century before AD 70, Jerusalem families collected a loved one’s bones after the flesh had decayed and put them in small limestone boxes, often scratched with names. Hundreds are known, with names such as Mary, Joseph, Simon, Jesus and Lazarus.
It shows how ordinary the Gospel names were. Jesus’ burial in a tomb, and the Gospels’ concern about uncleanness from graves, make more sense against this background.
Caution: An ossuary reading “Jesus son of Joseph” is real but means little: both names were common.

e.n: The crucified man of Giv’at ha-Mivtar
t: A heel bone from an ossuary in a Jerusalem tomb was pierced by an 11.5 cm iron nail, with traces of olive wood still attached. The ossuary was inscribed “Yehohanan”. It is the only skeletal remains of a crucified man known from Roman Judea.
It shows that crucifixion in Judea involved nails, as in John’s account of the marks on Jesus’ hands and feet, and that the victim could be buried by his family in a family tomb.
Caution: Original claims about how he was positioned were revised in 1985. Its date and the nail’s role are still debated.

A deep well inside a Greek Orthodox church marks the traditional spot, honored since at least the 4th century. It is fed by groundwater and was once about 40 m (130 ft) deep. A church was built here around AD 380 and rebuilt several times.
John says the woman was surprised that Jesus, with no bucket, could draw water: “the well is deep.” The site is also in the heart of Samaritan country, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
Caution: This is one of the few Gospel sites with a continuous, undisputed tradition.
f: Church from about AD 380; well deep in antiquity

t: Excavators found a large sacred precinct on the summit with a temple platform, altars and hundreds of inscriptions in Aramaic and Hebrew. John Hyrcanus destroyed it about 111 BC. The Samaritans still make Passover offerings on the mountain.
The Samaritan woman asks Jesus whether people should worship on “this mountain” or in Jerusalem. The hostility behind that question was centuries old.
f: Temple precinct built about 200 BC; destroyed about 111 BC

t: Herod rebuilt the old city of Samaria as Sebaste, honoring Augustus, with a temple, a forum, a stadium, a colonnaded street and strong walls. Its Roman ruins still stand on a hilltop.
Jesus travelled “between Samaria and Galilee,” and Samaria was home to the people he made the heroes of two stories. The Gospels never name this city.
Caution: It shows Samaria’s Roman-era setting; no Gospel event happens here.
A large Greek-style city below a mound, with a well-preserved Roman theater, a colonnaded street, bathhouses and a hippodrome. It was the only Decapolis city west of the Jordan.

The Gospels say crowds from the Decapolis followed Jesus, and the healed man proclaimed his story across the region. These cities were Greek in culture, showing a different world from the Jewish villages of Galilee.
Caution: Gospel texts do not mention Scythopolis by name.
The Roman city at Tyre has a vast hippodrome, a long colonnaded road and large cemeteries. It was a great Phoenician port long before and after Jesus.
Jesus withdraws to the district of Tyre and Sidon and meets a Gentile woman whose faith he praises. He also remarks that Tyre and Sidon would have repented had they seen the signs he did in Galilee.
Caution: Most of what is visible is later than Jesus.
f: Roman city; excavated colonnades from the 2nd–4th century

t: Emmaus-Nicopolis (Imwas) has a Roman city and Byzantine church, Abu Ghosh a Crusader church, Qubeibeh a Franciscan shrine over a Roman villa. Another candidate, Motza, is only about 6 km from Jerusalem.
Luke says Emmaus was “about seven miles from Jerusalem” (60 stadia), though some early manuscripts say 160 stadia. The village’s identity is unsettled.
Caution: Nobody knows which Emmaus it was.
f: Roman and Byzantine remains at several sites

t: Two tiny rolled silver amulets, found in a burial cave, carry the priestly blessing “The Lord bless you and keep you” in ancient Hebrew script. They are the oldest known fragments of any biblical text.
The blessing is the one priests spoke over the people. In Luke, Zechariah is a priest, and the risen Jesus lifts his hands in blessing as he leaves.
Caution: They are from the First Temple period, long before the Gospels.

Excavations at the mounds of Kuyunjik and Nebi Yunus uncovered the palaces of the Assyrian kings and the library of Ashurbanipal, with tens of thousands of clay tablets. Parts were badly damaged in 2014–17.
Jesus says the people of Nineveh will stand up at the judgement because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, and “something greater than Jonah is here”.

e.n: Papyri, contracts and phylacteries from the Judean desert
t: Dry caves have preserved legal papyri: marriage contracts, land deeds and certificates of divorce, along with tiny leather phylactery boxes holding Scripture, used for prayer.

They show how often marriage and divorce were a legal matter, which sheds light on the Pharisees’ question about divorce. Phylacteries and tassels explain Jesus’ remark about people who make theirs wide.

e.n: Stone vessels: cups and jars that stay clean
t: Cups, mugs and large jars were turned or carved from soft chalkstone, which Jewish law considered immune to ritual impurity. They appear in huge numbers in Jerusalem, Galilee and Judea in Jesus’ time. The big jars hold roughly 80–120 liters.
John mentions six stone water jars used for purification at the wedding in Cana. They are right for the setting and for the amount of wine Jesus made.

Hundreds of stepped, plastered pools have been found in Jerusalem, Qumran, Sepphoris, Magdala and Gamla, with private ones in rich houses and public ones near the Temple. Most have a divided stairway, one side for going down, one for coming up.
They were used to become ritually clean. They explain the washings the Gospels mention, the question about hand-washing and the baptism of John.
Small, hand-sized clay lamps, with a round body and a pinched spout (the “Herodian lamp”), are among the most common finds. A lamp burned a little olive oil for an hour or two.
Jesus’ images of lamps are everyday ones: lamps are put on a stand, kept filled while waiting for the bridegroom, and used to see the room.

e.n: Wine and oil presses, vineyards and terraces
t: Rock-cut treading floors with collecting vats, watchtowers and stone terraces survive across the hills of Judea and Galilee, along with stone olive-crushing basins and beam presses.
Vineyards and olive groves were common, so Jesus’ parable of the tenants builds a wall, a winepress and a tower for the vineyard, as every listener would have known.
Smooth, rock-cut circles on hilltops were used to thresh and winnow grain, and rock-cut pits and stone-lined silos stored it.
John the Baptist’s picture of wheat gathered into the barn while the chaff burns, the parable of the weeds, and the rich man’s plan to build bigger barns all use these familiar scenes.
Heavy basalt rotary querns, turned by hand or hourglass mills turned by donkeys, are common finds. A great millstone weighed as much as a person could carry.

Jesus’ warning about anyone who causes a child to stumble, that it would be better to have a great millstone hung around the neck, and his picture of two women grinding at the mill, use daily household tools.

Galilean homes were small basalt or fieldstone rooms around a shared courtyard, with flat roofs of beams, branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair. In Jerusalem’s Upper City, wealthy homes had mosaics, dining rooms and private baths.
A paralyzed man’s friends can tear through a roof, a woman can sweep her house for a lost coin, and a wise builder digs down to rock, because Jesus’ audience lived in houses like these.
Rome paved and marked key routes, with milestones, and Herod’s sons collected tolls where roads crossed borders. Capernaum lay on the road between Antipas’s Galilee and Philip’s territory.
This is the world of Levi (Matthew) sitting at his toll booth, of Zacchaeus the chief tax collector, and of the soldier who could make you carry his pack one mile.
Caution: Customs stations are described in writing; none from the Gospel period has been excavated at Capernaum.

Wealthy houses in Jerusalem’s Upper City had dining rooms with frescoed walls, mosaic floors, private ritual baths and imported tableware. Jewish custom at Passover was to recline on couches around the table. Josephus says the priests counted over 250,000 lambs offered one year.
John 13–17 is set around the Last Supper, and John says one disciple was “reclining next to Jesus”. The farewell conversations in John 14–17 take place within this meal setting.
Caution: The Gospels do not say whose house it was or where. This shows only what a dining room of the time looked like.
Josephus says priestly families kept careful written genealogies.
Stone benches in first-century synagogues show where Jews prayed and gathered.
Many excavated homes rest on bedrock or stone, the kind the wise builder chose.
Ancient terraces and presses show how central grapes and figs were to Galilee.
Ruins at Umm Qais include a theater, a colonnaded street and tombs.
Small bronze coins like the assarion are what Jesus says buys a sparrow.
Early synagogues have been found across Galilee, at places like Gamla and Magdala.
A boat found in the lake mud in 1986 shows how Jesus could teach from one.
Ruins at Al-Mina include Roman columns and a wide colonnaded road.
Excavations show Roman streets, columns and a huge hippodrome.
Roman-era ruins show a wealthy port city whose people came to hear Jesus.
At Banias, a cave and temple niches honor Pan beside a spring below Mount Hermon.
Tyrian silver coins, like the one in the fish, are common finds in Jerusalem.
Ancient weights show how large sums were measured, a talent being about 75 pounds.
Surviving first-century papyri include marriage contracts and divorce certificates.
Silver denarii with Tiberius’ image have been found across Judea.
Excavated palaces show the wealth of the road’s last stop.
Palaces at Tulul Abu el-Alayiq show the wealth of Herod’s winter capital.
Excavated winter palaces near Jericho show how rich the town was.
Tyrian silver shekels, used for the temple tax, are common finds in Jerusalem.
Monumental tombs in the Kidron Valley, like Zechariah’s, honor Jerusalem’s dead.
Tiny leather cases with Scripture scrolls were found in the Judean desert.
Small clay lamps with a spout are common finds across Judea.
An ossuary inscribed with Caiaphas’ family name was found in Jerusalem.
A heel bone pierced by a nail was found in a Jerusalem tomb of this era.
A heel bone with an iron nail was found in a Jerusalem tomb of this era.
A crucified man’s heel bone, with a nail, was found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1968.
Round stones that rolled in a groove sealed some Jerusalem tombs.
Round stones in a groove sealed some Jerusalem tombs.
Rock-cut tombs of the time were sealed with rolling disk stones, as in the story.
A later white limestone synagogue stands over the first-century basalt one.
An early house church was built over a home in Capernaum.
Capernaum houses were small basalt homes around shared courtyards.
Customs stations stood along the lakeshore road near Capernaum.
Early synagogues at Gamla and Magdala show where such teaching happened.
The shoreline near Tabgha has ancient harbor structures.
A fifth-century church holds a mosaic of loaves and fish on the shore.
A church beside the lake honors the breakfast Jesus served.
Cave tombs cut into hillsides are common around the lake.
Rich men’s rock-cut tombs near Jerusalem show how wealth marked even burial.
A cave and spring below Hermon preserve niches for the god Pan.
A paved Roman road ran up from Jericho to Jerusalem.
Tiny bronze coins of this era are common finds in Jerusalem.
Built under Constantine, rebuilt in the 6th century.
Small perfume flasks like the woman’s are common finds from first-century sites.
Rock-cut pits and silos show how large landowners stored their grain.
Wealthy homes in Jerusalem had dining rooms built for reclining guests.
Silver drachmas like the lost coin were worth about a day’s wage.
Stone olive presses across Galilee show how important oil was for trade.
Ancient Jericho’s mound is among the oldest cities known, but Jesus’ Jericho lay nearby.
Herod’s winter palaces near Jericho have been excavated, with pools and gardens.
Herod’s builders cut enormous blocks, some weighing hundreds of tons.
Tiny bronze lepta have been found in Jerusalem, many no bigger than a fingernail.
Several places claim to be Emmaus, including Emmaus-Nicopolis and Abu Ghosh.
Stepped ritual baths are found across Jerusalem from this period.
Excavations on Gerizim uncovered a Samaritan temple platform.
Two large pools with colonnades were found near St. Anne’s Church.
Later Roman shrines to Asclepius stood nearby.
Broad stairs on the south side led pilgrims up to the temple.
Broad steps on the temple platform’s south side lead to the old Huldah Gates.
Chambers along the Court of Women held the offering chests.
The eastern wall of Herod’s platform stands near where Solomon’s Porch was.
Rock-cut folds and cisterns survive in the Judean hills.
A rock-cut tomb in al-Eizariya has been honored as Lazarus’ tomb since early times.
Alabaster flasks for costly perfume are found in Jerusalem tombs.
The ancient road down the Mount of Olives into the city still survives in part.
The traditional room, called the Cenacle, stands in the Crusader-era building.
Stone and clay basins for foot washing are found in wealthy Jerusalem homes.
Houses in Jerusalem’s upper city had multiple rooms around a courtyard.
Rock-cut presses and vats appear in vineyards across Judea.
Early synagogues at Masada and Herodium show how Jewish communities gathered.
Breastplate stones of twelve tribes are described in Exodus 28.
Excavations on Mount Zion reveal large first-century homes of the priestly aristocracy.
Rock-cut tombs with rolling stones are found around Jerusalem.
Betrothal was legally binding, so ending it took a formal divorce.
Jewish family lists usually named fathers only, so Matthew’s four women stand out.
Magi were scholar-priests who studied stars and dreams, likely from Persia.
Gold, frankincense and myrrh were costly gifts, fit for a king.
John’s camel-hair clothes and leather belt matched Elijah’s, a deliberate prophetic sign.
Locusts were a clean food under the Law and a common desert meal.
Flat round loaves were the daily staple, so turning stones to bread meant ending hunger.
Fishermen cast round nets by hand, then mended them on the shore.
A rabbi sat to teach with authority, so Jesus visibly takes that role.
Anointing the head with oil was normal grooming, so fasting should look ordinary.
Spices honored the dead and eased the smell, they did not preserve the body.
Walled towns had narrow gates, so the road through one was tight and easy to miss.
Sudden rains turned dry riverbeds into torrents that swept away poor foundations.
A healed leper brought offerings to the priest, as the Law of Moses required.
Banquet guests lay on couches, so “reclining with Abraham” pictures a feast of honor.
Flat roofs of beams and clay could be opened, as when friends lowered the paralytic.
Roofs were beams covered with branches and clay, so a crowd could open one.
Flute players and wailing mourners were hired at a death, so they were already there.
Traveling light made the Twelve depend on each town’s hospitality.
Shaking dust from the feet marked leaving non-Jewish land, so here it was a solemn warning.
Shaking dust off the feet marked leaving non-Jewish land, so here it was a pointed warning.
Village children played at weddings and funerals, the image Jesus uses for a stubborn crowd.
Pharisees counted plucking grain as reaping, work the Sabbath forbade.
Most rabbis allowed rescuing a sheep on the Sabbath, which Jesus uses in His answer.
The weeds were likely darnel, which looks like wheat until it matures.
A public oath was hard to break without losing face, so Herod gave the order.
The fourth watch came before dawn, so Jesus reached them in the last hours of night.
Ritual hand washing before meals was a tradition, not a command of Moses.
Pharisees washed before meals for purity, so Jesus skipping it was noticed.
Declaring money “Corban” set it aside for God, a loophole to avoid supporting parents.
Calling goods “Corban” dedicated them to God, which some used to avoid helping parents.
Keys marked a steward’s authority over a house, as in Isaiah 22.
Peter’s offer of shelters recalls the booths built at the Feast of Tabernacles.
Peter’s offer to build shelters recalls the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles.
A stater was a silver coin worth four drachmas, enough for two men’s temple tax.
Children had no status in the ancient world, so honoring one was a shock.
A husband gave a written divorce certificate, which let the wife remarry.
The camel was the largest animal in Galilee, so the image is deliberately absurd.
The day counted from sunrise, so the eleventh hour was near sunset.
A king on a donkey meant peace, not war, unlike a king on a war horse.
Spreading cloaks and branches on the road honored a king.
Guests were expected to dress properly for a wedding feast, as a sign of respect.
A childless widow married her husband’s brother to carry on the family line.
A childless widow married her husband’s brother to continue the family line.
Tombs were whitewashed so travelers wouldn’t touch them and become unclean.
Flat roofs were living space with outside stairs, so fleeing meant not going back inside.
Travel on the Sabbath was limited, which would make a Sabbath flight harder.
Small clay lamps burned only a short while, so spare oil was needed.
A talent was a huge sum, roughly many years of a laborer’s pay.
At Passover guests reclined at table, so a dipped bowl was shared closely.
Guests reclined at the table, so those beside Jesus shared the same dish.
Guests reclined at meals with feet to the side, so the woman could reach Jesus’ feet.
A prisoner was released at the festival, a gesture to calm the crowds.
Bodies were wrapped in cloth and laid in rock-cut tombs sealed with a stone.
Women’s testimony carried little weight in court, yet they are first at the tomb.
Spices and perfumes were brought to honor the body, not to preserve it.
Camel hair and a leather belt recalled the prophet Elijah.
Teachers usually quoted earlier rabbis, but Jesus spoke on His own authority.
Roofs of beams, branches and clay could be opened from above.
Roofs were living space with outside stairs, so fleeing meant not going back in.
Old skins grew stiff and would burst if filled with fermenting wine.
Many rabbis allowed healing on the Sabbath only to save a life.
Family was a person’s greatest loyalty, so Jesus’ words shocked.
Farmers scattered seed by hand before plowing it under.
The curved shore works like an amphitheater, carrying a voice across the water.
Hillside caves served as tombs, and touching the dead made one unclean.
A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and kept apart.
Shaking dust off one’s feet signaled a break with a town.
A king could not easily take back a vow made in front of guests.
Washing hands, cups and couches was a Pharisaic tradition, not a Mosaic command.
A little leaven spreads through all the dough, standing for hidden influence.
Saliva was a folk remedy, though Jesus needed no such help.
Teachers were often given children to bless, though disciples tried to block them.
Spreading cloaks and leafy branches on the road honored a king.
A king on a donkey came in peace, not on a war horse.
Landowners often leased vineyards, collecting a share of the fruit.
The smallest coins in use, worth a fraction of a day’s wage.
Roman time divided night into four watches, and servants stayed alert.
Prisoners were beaten before crucifixion, often weakening them.
A written charge was fixed above the condemned person on the cross.
Work stopped from Friday sunset, so the women waited until Sunday.

The list of books accepted as Scripture. The four Gospels were widely read and accepted as authoritative by the second century. Christian groups differ over some Old Testament books.
The study of ancient manuscripts to work out the wording of the original text. No original manuscripts of the Gospels survive, but thousands of copies do, and most differences between them are small.

A language related to Hebrew that was the everyday speech of most Jews in Judea and Galilee. Jesus probably spoke it daily. The Gospels preserve a few of his Aramaic words, such as Talitha cumi, Ephphatha, Abba and Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani.
The common Greek of the Mediterranean world in the first century, in which all four Gospels were written. The Greek word studies in this app use it.
A translation approach that stays as close as possible to the wording and structure of the original, even when it sounds less natural in English. Examples: KJV, ASV, NASB, ESV.
A translation approach that aims to convey the meaning of the original in natural English, even if the wording changes. Also called functional equivalence. Examples: NIV, NLT (in part).
A free restatement in the translator’s own words, more like a commentary than a translation. Examples: The Message, The Living Bible.
The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, made in Alexandria from about the 3rd century BC. Most Old Testament quotations in the New Testament follow it.
The Latin Bible translated mainly by Jerome around AD 382 to 405. It was the Bible of Western Christianity for a thousand years.

The traditional Hebrew text of the Old Testament, copied and preserved by Jewish scribes (the Masoretes) between about the 7th and 10th centuries AD. Most English Old Testaments are translated from it.

Manuscripts found from 1947 in caves near Qumran, dating from about the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD. They include every Old Testament book except Esther and show that the Hebrew text was copied very faithfully.

A 4th-century Greek manuscript containing most of the Old Testament and the whole New Testament, discovered at St. Catherine’s Monastery on Mount Sinai. One of the oldest and most important Bible manuscripts.
A 4th-century Greek manuscript of the Bible kept in the Vatican Library, among the oldest and most important surviving manuscripts.

The Greek New Testament text published by Erasmus in 1516 and revised by others, based on a handful of late manuscripts. The King James Version and NKJV are based on it. Most modern translations use a critical text drawn from earlier manuscripts.
A Greek New Testament assembled by scholars comparing thousands of manuscripts (Nestle-Aland, UBS). Most modern translations use it.
